speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-93, to amend the Freight Rates Reduction Act.
He said: I have a few brief remarks to make. Quite an extensive study was given to the resolution that preceded this bill, and there is very little additional information I can give that was not given on the resolution.
As the house knows, the Freight Rates Reduction Act was passed in 1959. Its purpose was to alleviate the burden of the 17 per cent general freight rate increase authorized in

November, 1958. The rates to which the act applies are the normal class rates and commodity rates, excepting competitive rates, which were taking the 17 per cent increase on the day the act came into force.
Class rates are the maximum rates that the railways can charge. They apply to about 8,000 articles in the Canadian freight classification. The principal articles shipped at class rates are high class manufactured articles.
Commodity rates are lower than the class rates, and they apply on bulk commodities and other articles shipped in large quantities such as steel, sand and gravel, lumber, pulp-wood, fruits and vegetables, ores, cement, wood pulp, newsprint paper, canned goods, sugar and so forth.
The reduction required by the act does not apply to subnormal rates which the railways have published because of competition, such as competitive rates and agreed charges. Neither does it apply to the statutory Crows-nest pass grain and flour rates, nor to international rates between Canada and the United States, nor to export and import traffic carried at rates in competition with United States ports.
The act made provision for the board of transport commissioners to require reductions to be made in the class and commodity rates, other than competitive rates, that were in effect and taking the 17 per cent increase on the day the act came into force. The reductions were to be effective during a period of not more than one year. Provision was made for payments not exceeding $20 million to reimburse the companies for the resulting reduction in their revenues.
The act came into force on July 8, 1959. The first reduction in the freight rates became effective on August 1, 1959, when the 17 per cent increase was reduced by 7 percentage points; in other words, it became 10 per cent instead of 17 per cent. In the following spring the board ordered a further reduction of two more percentage points, bringing the 17 per cent increase down to 8 per cent. It has remained at that level ever since.
The act was amended last year by extending the one year period of the reductions for another nine months and by increasing the $20 million by another $15 million, making a total of $35 million for the full 21 months.
The purpose of the amendment is to extend the provisions of the act for a further period not exceeding 12 months from April 30 last. The original bill and last year's amending bill were considered at length by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of the house and also by the standing committee on transport and communications of the Senate. There is no
Freight Rates Reduction Act change in the principle or purpose of the legislation at this time. What is proposed is a continuation of its provisions for a further period of 12 months. After the present discussion I propose to move that the bill be referred to the standing committee which I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday there was a general discussion on the resolution to amend the Freight Rates Reduction Act, and I do not want to traverse the ground covered then. However, there are a number of things that remain to be said in connection with the bill now before the house.
In my view the bill divides itself into two parts. First, it authorizes the board of transport commissioners to make an order continuing the freight rates reduction which was authorized under an earlier act in 1960. Second, it attempts, although I doubt whether it succeeds, to make the rates retroactive. In so far as the shipper is concerned, I do not think there can be any doubt that the reduction is effective. In so far as the railways are concerned, I believe there is some doubt, and I should like the minister to clarify that position when we get to clause 1 of the bill.
My understanding of the situation is that the railways may, if they wish, file a tariff in reduction of rates, but that the board of transport commissioners cannot in any way make that tariff retroactive. That is why I said earlier that so far as the shipper is concerned the moment the railways file a tariff in reduction of rates or in continuation of a rate reduction, that position is covered, but I do not think that applies with respect to the board of transport commissioners. I said that I do not think they can either make a rate retroactive or payments retroactive, and on that point I should like to get some clarification later.
A question was also raised by the Leader of the Opposition in connection with the statement made by the Prime Minister, and there was no explanation given by the minister yesterday when he rose to reply on the resolution. I refer, of course, to the statement that appears in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 25, wherein the Prime Minister said that the subsidy would be retroactive, and I quote from this dispatch from Ottawa:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker said Friday legislation to extend the $20 million a year rollback subsidy on freight rates will be made retroactive to May 1 when it is passed by parliament.
Then there is this significant passage:
He said the government notice given the commons earlier this week would act in the same way as a budget proposal which becomes effective when it is announced, subject to later parliamentary approval.

Freight Rates Reduction Act
Of course that is not the case, and I think the minister owes it to the house to deal with this matter. The notice referred to by the Prime Minister is certainly not in the nature of a budget proposal, nor has it the same effect, nor does it come into effect until both houses of parliament have approved the legislation and it has been proclaimed. Therefore I think the house is entitled to an explanation of that statement.
However, sir, I rose for another purpose this morning, namely to deal with some of the statements which were made yesterday during the course of the debate and particularly with a statement made by the minister which I will put on the record in a moment. During the course of the reply made by the minister the inference was left that while we were in office little or nothing was done in connection with this whole very serious matter of freight rate reduction and the freight rate structure. I quote what the minister said, as found on page 4836 of Hansard:
I should just like to present certain figures at this time, which I am not pulling out of a hat, in respect of those figures quoted this afternoon. I suggest by looking at the varying proportions regarding freight rate increases we will then have a clearer picture in respect of which government is more concerned with the welfare of Canadian citizens as far as freight rates are concerned.
Since 1945 freight rates have increased by 157 per cent. One hundred and forty per cent of this increase occurred during the time my hon. friend was a minister under the Liberal regime.
I pause here to state that while I am unable to verify the increase of 157 per cent I take it that perhaps it is correct, but I do make the statement that if freight rates have risen by that amount in Canada they have risen by a higher amount in the United States and by an equal amount in the United Kingdom. So, having regard to the kind of economy existing in those countries, there is not too much to-I am looking for a better word than "blow" about, because I do not want to inject a note of contention into the debate.

speechtext: Oh, go ahead.

speechtext:
From the statement the minister made, and with which I am dealing now, I do not think there is too much for him to become exercised about, because the position is no better here than it is elsewhere. The minister went on to say:
During the Conservative administration-that is during the last four years-the only increase which has been allowed was to the extent of 10 per cent, which was later reduced to 8 per cent. In other words, the total increase of 171 per cent was originally decreased to 10 per cent, and then to 8 per cent. The government has also frozen all increases: this policy is still in effect. I suggest that this government has shown the people of Canada what it thought of the great burden of freight rates in various parts of the country.
fMr. Chevrier.]

This government has looked into the matter seriously and has gone out of its way in an attempt to help the shippers of various regions of Canada, who have had to face these freight rate increases.
I should like to tell the minister that the former administration not only did what he said but went a great deal further. As I said earlier, from this statement of the minister the inference is created that little or nothing was done by the previous administration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I hear cries of "hear, hear" from the other side of the house. I should like to put on the record some of the things that were done. It would take too much time to go into them seriatim, but in the light of what was said yesterday and the fact that this is a debate on freight rates there are some general statements which I think deserve to be put on the record.
First of all, let me say that there were no increases in freight rates in this country for quite a long time. From 1903 until world war I there were no increases whatsoever in freight rates in Canada. The first general increase came in 1917. I need not tell the house what government was in office then. The increase amounted to 15 per cent. The second came one year later in 1918, and amounted to 25 per cent. It was made not by the board of transport commissioners but by a cabinet direction given to the board. An order in council was passed by the government of the day, which was a Conservative administration, directing the board of transport commissioners to increase freight rates to the extent of 25 per cent. In 1920, still under a Conservative administration, there was an increase of 40 per cent in the freight rates of this country following an application made by the railway association of Canada to the board of transport commissioners.
Then there was a change of administration. When the Liberal government took office the 40 per cent increase which had been approved in 1920 was reduced first by a 5 per cent decrease in 1921 and then by a 10 per cent decrease in the same year. This was followed by a further decrease on August 1, 1922 leaving, in respect of the 40 per cent increase, a net increase of 17J per cent in eastern Canada and 12J per cent in western Canada.
Turning now to another aspect of this question I wish to deal with the manner in which freight rates and the freight rate structure were dealt with in former years. I need hardly tell the house that the Crowsnest rates were established in 1897. They were perhaps the lowest grain rates in the world. They were so considered at the time and they have never been touched or tampered with, with

but one exception. There is some reference to those rates in the recommendations contained in the first volume of the report of the MacPherson commission. From the representations that were made to the royal commission by various groups all across Canada it is quite clear that even at this date, 64 years later, there is a jealous regard for those rates. There is, too, a general view, particularly in the prairie provinces, that they should not be touched.
In 1903 the Railway Act was enacted in this country. It established the board of transport commissioners, giving that board powers to deal with applications concerning freight rates. In 1924 there was inaugurated a freight rate investigation to determine whether it was possible to equalize freight rates in Canada. I bring to the attention of the house that in 1924 and even long before that, as I shall be able to show later on, there was an attempt in this country to equalize freight rates; so that when we are told in the house that the MacPherson commission on transportation is going to bring in a recommendation to equalize freight rates we should not become too excited over that because the board of transport commissioners, royal commissions and other investigations have over many years dealt with this very difficult and complex question of the equalization of freight rates.
In 1927 the then administration introduced the Maritime Freight Rates Act giving the benefit of a 20 per cent reduction in freight rates to the select maritime region. That has since been increased to 30 per cent under a Liberal regime.
From 1948 to 1950, over a series of various steps, the mountain differential was entirely removed. Following this, under an order in council known as P.C. 1487 the board of transport commissioners was authorized to make a thorough investigation into the rate structure of railways and railway companies with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure which would, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities so as to permit the freest possible interchange of commodities between various provinces and the extension of Canadian trade both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of agriculture and other basic commodities.
In 1948 there was established by the former government a royal commission on transportation or, if you prefer to call it such, the Turgeon commission. That commission sat for a period of more than two years and brought in a very exhaustive report, one of the finest ever produced on the subject of freight rates, together with that of the Duff commission.
Freight Rates Reduction Act The two, taken together, are historic documents which will stand out for many years to come, and which I submit have been a tremendous benefit to the railways, to the shippers and to the taxpayers of this country. I am not suggesting that the MacPherson commission will not bring in an equally good report, but the house will have to await the publication of the subsequent two volumes before an opinion can be expressed in that connection.
The Turgeon commission made an exhaustive study. It was made by a person who had devoted a great deal of his life to problems concerning western Canada, and who was praised for the recommendations contained in his report by the present Prime Minister when he sat on this side of the house as a private member. Finally in 1951 the then government accepted the recommendations of the Turgeon commission. All of them which had to do with freight rates, and many others incidental thereto, were brought into effect by way of legislation implementing those recommendations. It was stated at the time on both sides of the house that this was the most important and most forward looking piece of legislation having to do with freight rates ever introduced in the house.
What did this legislation do? First, it provided in accordance with the recommendations of the Turgeon commission for the payment of a subsidy of several million dollars to maintain the trackage through northern Ontario which serves as a link or bridge between certain points in northern Ontario. Second, it provided for a national freight rate policy as enacted in section 336 of the Railway Act. This was an over-all direction to the board of transport commissioners stating that every railway company, in the language of that section:
-shall, so far as is reasonably possible, in respect of all freight traffic of the same description, and carried on or upon the like kind of cars or conveyances, passing over all lines or routes of the company in Canada, charge tolls to all persons at the same rate, whether by weight, mileage or otherwise.
This, of course, is subject to the exceptions mentioned in subsection 4 of section 336. This section was of tremendous benefit to western Canada. It provided for equalization of rates between the east and west, and also paved the way for equalization of certain commodities.
Another feature of this legislation was the one and one third rule which is contained in section 337 of the Railway Act. The legislation also provided for uniform classification of a system of accounts for the railways. The interstate commerce commission had led the way or had used this system for years; and
4880	HOUSE OF
Freight Rates Reduction Act because, as the house knows, railways in Canada-the C.N.R., the C.P.R. and others- moved to points in the United States, it was felt by the royal commission that there should be a uniform method of accounting for these lines. The legislation provided for the filing of a competitive tariff before the board so that the board could go into such and such a rate and ascertain that it was bona fide and compensatory. It also provided for the recapitalization of the C.N.R. and other matters which it would take too long for me to go into at the present time.
Before I go on to another point I should like to acquaint the minister with the attitude taken by the opposition at that time. I do not know whether or not he was in the house then, but I believe he was. The opposition took a very negative attitude toward some of the measures that were brought forward, notwithstanding the fact that the present Prime Minister had declared that this report of the royal commission was an excellent one.
The opposition first of all sought to do away with the board of transport commissioners. When the estimates of the Department of Transport were up for consideration, the opposition moved that the item be reduced to $1. I will not mention the names of those who were prominent in that discussion. That attempt was not successful, of course, but it gave some indication of what was in the minds of the members of the opposition at that time. Not only did they move to reduce to $1 the estimates for the maintenance and operation of the board of transport commissioners, but they condemned the board of transport commissioners, and some of them would have done away with the board. It was said by them that the board was incompetent, that it was responsible for the state of confusion and chaos in which the country found itself, that it was not functioning as it should function, that it was not competent to assume its task. That language can be found at page 3121 of Hansard of June 2, 1950.
May I point out that this government has been in office now for four years. If it had wished to do so, it could have done something about the board of transport commissioners in those four years. The fact that it has maintained the board is evidence that the criticism made by it in the days when it was in opposition was futile and really of no use. In those days the opposition were opposed to the establishment of the royal commission. They fought the royal commission. They said a royal commission to deal with freight rates was useless. They said it was a complete waste of time. Although the provinces wanted a royal commission, the then leader of the opposition did not want one.
[Mr. Chevrier.l

speechtext: What was the name of the leader of the opposition then?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
Hon. Mr. Drew. He made statements declaring himself to be against a royal commission to deal with this allimportant subject. However, because of the attitude taken by the provinces and by most of the responsible groups in Canada, the Conservative party changed its attitude and at its convention passed a resolution demanding a royal commission, thereby overruling its leader. There was in those days in the opposition, as there is today in the government, evidence of confusion and of party members running in two directions at the same time. We have had examples of that situation, and we certainly have had an example of confusion and chaos in connection with this whole problem.
A great deal has been said about horizontal increases in freight rates and about their unjust, unfair, and inequitable impact upon all parts of Canada. With regard to that statement there can be no objection or no complaint. That is a fact. When freight rates are raised horizontally they are bound to create inequity in certain parts of Canada that are far away from markets. However, that is not a new position. That position has existed in this country for many years. That position was dealt with by the royal commission on transportation headed by Mr. Turgeon.
The Prime Minister has indicated that when the MacPherson royal commission hands down its report, a formula will be found whereby freight rates across Canada can be equalized and therefore the impact of horizontal increases in rates can be minimized or made to disappear entirely, thus by inference leading us to believe that no previous attempt has been made at equalization. I want to correct that suggestion. I should like to put on record what Mr. Justice Turgeon had to say in his royal commission report in 1951. At page 50, in chapter 2, under the heading "Horizontal Increases", we find the following:
The method of applying a uniform percentage increase to all rates is known as the "horizontal percentage increase".
The seven provinces which opposed the 30 per cent and 20 per cent increase applications before the board from 1946 to 1950 and attacked the horizontal increase method continued their attack before this commission.
It can thus be seen that the matter of horizontal increases is not a new one. I continue the quotation:
Many submissions were made criticizing this method and asserting that it works great hardship upon shippers in the provinces subject to long haul on their traffic.
Then the commissioner goes on to give examples of horizontal increases in freight

rates. Then at page 52, under the heading "Treatment of the Subject by the Duncan Commission", I find the following:
The following excerpts from the report of the Duncan commission seem to indicate the importance of this subject.
In the report which was made in September 1926 appear the following statements:
"Incidence of horizontal war increases"
"There is one further very important feature of the railway situation as it affects the maritimes, which calls for special attention. In one sense it is connected with the problems that we have been discussing, but its immediate incidence is not so interconnected with the general problem as to make it impossible to deal with it separately. Indeed the reaction of the burden which it imposes is so great that, in our view, it should be dealt with as a special problem. We refer to the system under which, during the late war, flat percentage increases (known as horizontal increases) were added to railway rates."
I refer to that passage in passing simply in order to show that as far back as 1926 the Duncan commission took cognizance of this matter. The chief commissioner goes on at some length to deal with the manner in which this question is handled in the United States, and I shall not refer to that matter. However, he draws a number of interesting conclusions which I should like to put on the record now. First, he states at page 61 of the report:
Applications for uniform horizontal increases to all freight tolls assume that all freight can, under all conditions, bear an equal burden of increase. This is an incorrect assumption.
2.	Horizontal increases, although preserving rate relationships percentagewise, disturb them in cents per 100 pounds (or other unit) in so far as shippers and consignees are concerned, and this is of much importance to them.
3.	Horizontal increases aggravate the disadvantage already suffered by long haul shippers and consignees.
4.	The remedy does not lie in the prohibition, statutory or other, of horizontal increases, but is in the hands of the railways themselves. The railways should make studies of traffic conditions in all their bearings and should present to the board (in accordance with the foregoing precedents) proposals showing not only their maximum percentage increase requirement, but also, among other particulars, varying percentage increases on different commodities, flat, instead of percentage increases when these are more suitable, and maxima in appropriate cases in cents per 100 pounds or other unit. Special attention should be given to long haul traffic and to rates on basic (or primary) commodities. The railways should be in a position to do this especially in the light of new statistical procedures. But if the railways do not approach the task in this way, it ought to be the duty of the board to see that they do so. Presumably an examination of the "waybill study" undertaken by the board will help to provide it with the requisite "reliable traffic statistics" which it stated were lacking in the 30 per cent applications.
Finally the commissioner concludes by saying that legislative enactments to deal with this are not necessary. At this stage I should like to show what was done by the
Freight Rates Reduction Act board of transport commissioners following that recommendation and following the legislation which was introduced in the house by the former administration to equalize freight rates across this country.
I mentioned earlier that under order in council P.C. 1487 the government had directed the board of transport commissioners to conduct an investigation into the whole subject of equalization. The first thing the board of transport commissioners did to comply with that recommendation was to ask the railways to make an analysis of the waybill, that is, a waybill study. As the house knows, there are some 65,000 or more different freight rates in Canada. Before it was possible for anybody, let alone the board of transport commissioners, to study this problem it was necessary to make a study and an analysis of the waybill. This the board of transport commissioners did, and they made an interim report on the equalization of freight rates which is dated Ottawa, March 25, 1955.
This report refers to the order in council which established the board to deal with the matter. It refers to section 336, which established the national freight policy in Canada. I should like to read this short paragraph from page 4 of the report:
The board completed the first phase of the equalization of freight rates on March 1, 1955, by establishing on that date a new freight classification and a new scheme of "class" rates applied in connection with that classification, and the present therefore appears to be an appropriate time at which to make an interim report in the matter of equalization generally.
Then it goes on to deal in detail with what had been done. I think it can be summed up by this sentence at page 17:
-it has been possible within two years to evolve finally a class rate scale which was thought worthy of being put into effect and subjected to the test of experience.
There then came a further report which is dated September 23, 1957 and which is signed by Clarence D. Shepard, the chief commissioner. I should have said that the earlier report dated March 25, 1955 was under the signature of the then chief commissioner, Mr. Justice Kearney. Page 1 of the report of 1957 states:
-the first phase of equalization throughout Canada, namely, of class rates accompanied by a new freight classification, had been accomplished and made effective on March 1, 1955.
The report states at page 4:
The equalized class rates have now been in effect for two and one half years and have cured the complaints that existed for so many years concerning the higher class rates in western Canada compared with eastern Canada.
Then it says that the second phase of equalization is to deal with commodity rates, which it divides into four classifications. The

Freight Rates Reduction Act report goes on to deal with those. There came a third report dated December 22, 1958, this one again signed by Clarence D. Shepard, the chief commissioner. I should like to put on Hansard the second introductory paragraph of this report:
Order in council P.C. 1487 of April 7, 1948 required a general investigation of the freight rate structure of Canada, and directed that this investigation be made "with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities, etc." Section 366 of the Railway Act is broader in its application and sets forth the national freight rate policy that, subject to certain exceptions, "every railway company shall, so far as is reasonably possible, in respect of all freight traffic of the same description, and carried on or upon the like kind of cars or conveyances, passing over all lines or routes of the company in Canada, charge tolls to all persons at the same rate, whether by weight, mileage or otherwise".
The board has been proceeding with "equalization" as defined by section 336, i.e., that subject to all reasonable considerations and the exceptions set forth in the section, the rate on a given article for the same distance and for the same weight must be the same in any part of Canada west of the maritime provinces, despite any differences in circumstances and conditions.
Then it lists the various -board judgments dealing with equalization and it gives a long list of articles upon which freight rates in Canada have been equalized. This report concludes by saying that in as far as it has been possible so to do, these rates have been equalized.
My purpose in putting these matters on the record is to indicate, first, that this was not a new subject; it dates back many, many years; that equalization has been going on in this country over a period of years; that equalization was recommended by the Turgeon commission and was put into effect by three interim reports of the board of transport commissioners thereby lightening, but not making disappear entirely the effect of horizontal freight rate increases.
I hope the present royal commission on transportation will be able to come up with a formula which will make horizontal freight rate increases disappear entirely and equalize freight rates to the fullest extent across this country. That would be a desirable objective. Whether it can be reached or not I am unable to say, but I do know that under the previous administration the board of transport commissioners gave this subject careful consideration, and anybody either in this house or outside who tries to say that the previous administration did not face up to this problem is making an inaccurate and false statement. I repeat that the recommendations are there; they are indicative of what was done by the royal commission. The legislation

also is there to indicate what was the attitude of the government. At that time there were various bills introduced in the house -I have forgotten how many, but certainly there were a number of them-dealing with each of the aspects upon which recommendations were made by the Turgeon commission. Will the present administration do the same thing? I invite them to do so when they have decided upon which parts of the report they intend to implement.
I leave the subject there, satisfied that I have replied effectively to any statement or charge, made directly or by inference, that little or nothing was done by those who were in office for 22 years. The record is there to bear me out. I think the previous administration did a great deal, both during the 22 years when the last Liberal government was in office and under earlier Liberal governments, to deal with this question, which is a complex one, a complicated one, and one which cannot be dealt with overnight. Having said that, I can only reiterate that we on this side of the house will give our full support to this measure, and hope it will be possible for the minister to clear up any doubts I have in mind about the retroactivity of this bill when we come to discuss it clause by clause.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would answer one supplementary question. 1 may have misunderstood him, but I understood the hon. member to say on one occasion that the Crowsnest pass freight rates were shackling the railways. That was at the time when the Prime Minister declared that the rates were a magna carta for western Canada. Did the hon. gentleman suggest in

this house at any time that the Crowsnest pass rates were shackling the railways and should be changed?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext: I thought I had answered that question by referring just now to statements I had made when I was sitting on the other side of the house. I have been in the house for 23 years and I do not remember all the statements I have made, but I cannot recall having made a statement of the nature quoted by the hon. gentleman or any statement like it having to do with the Crowsnest rates, and this is in line with the attitude I have taken all along. If, perchance, the hon. member is able to show that I have made such a statement I shall be the first to rise in the house and correct it. However, I should be tremendously surprised if any such statement was made either by me or by any member of the Liberal administration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
speechtext:
The question which the hon. member for Bow River put to the hon. member for Laurier is indeed an interesting one. Perhaps clearer than anything else in the discussion of freight rates one thing stands out, and that is the policy of every political party in Canada, as enunciated from time to time, that the Crowsnest rates must remain unchanged and must not be tampered with. Any government or any political party which embarked on a course of tampering with the Crowsnest rates so as to raise the rates on western grain would not have a chance to elect a single member from any one of the three prairie provinces. So if any political party in Canada wishes to commit suicide in the three prairie provinces, this is the course open to it and this is the way to bring it about.
As a matter of fact the people on the prairies are so much opposed to tampering with the Crowsnest rates that they would view very carefully any contention that those rates should be used in such a way as to get something for the railways by way of a compensatory grant. The railways require assistance. The employees who work for the railways should not be forced, as they have been in the past, to accept wages lower than those paid to workers in comparable industries. But the Crowsnest pass rates must remain as they are now and no method should be used by any government, either directly or indirectly, to undermine the effect of those rates.
There has been a great deal of speculation lately as to whether the country may be confronted with a fall election, and an atmosphere of this kind leads members in various part of the house to make speeches which are tailored to meet such a situation. I think this
Freight Rates Reduction Act present bill is tailored to that possibility. I do not say this bill means we are to have an election in the fall, but the government is taking no chances; the government is doing everything it can to make a fall election possible if it decides at some later date that an election at that time would be in its own political interest.
The long and carefully prepared speech which was read by the hon. member for Laurier certainly suggests to me that the Liberal party and its great research bureau are very conscious that an election may be coming before long, and in order to provide some alternative argument to this legislation or to the royal commission report which has been placed before the country the hon. member for Laurier has made a spirited and detailed defence of the Liberal party, not only of today but throughout its whole history. He has endeavoured to show that it is the Conservative party which has been the party of high freight rates and that it has been the Liberal party which has valiantly come to the rescue of the freight users of this country by taking far-reaching steps to equalize freight rates and relieve the burden caused by horizontal increases.
The Turgeon commission report was presented on February 9, 1951. From the end of the war until that time, according to the information I hold in my hand, and I believe it is correct, there were two horizontal increases in freight rates. On April 8, 1958 there was a 21 per cent increase; on June 16, 1950 there was a 20 per cent increase.
Then we received the report to which the hon. member for Laurier has referred. We have it. The government did a few things about it. Some measures were introduced, and after we had the report, on February 11, 1952 there was a 17 per cent increase in freight rates. On January 1, 1953 there was another 9 per cent increase; on March 16, 1953 a 7 per cent increase; on July 3, 1956 a 7 per cent interim increase; in December, 1956 the 7 per cent interim increase was increased to 11 per cent. We had a couple of increases before the report; we had four complete increases in a total of five stages after the report.
I am very much opposed to freight rate increases. I am disappointed that the government did not roll the last increase right back to the position before the increase, but we were getting dizzy with increased freight rates under the former administration. Although the royal commission report was pitchforked in among the increases, nevertheless the increases continued at a very alarming and rather monotonous rate.

Freight Rates Reduction Act
Well, the Liberal government had royal commissions and the Conservative government has had royal commissions. We have one now. The Turgeon royal commission made one report. It did not help very much. The MacPherson royal commission is going to make three reports, and I do not know whether the three reports of the MacPherson commission are going to be any more substantial in their effects than the one report of the Turgeon commission. We have the initial report of the MacPherson commission and, according to the government, all its railway freight policies were being tailored to the moment when the MacPherson commission would make its report. That is, both as to railway wage rates and as to freight rate policy, the government would get the report, it would make up its mind, it would study the report and it would act.
It received the report. Apparently it studied it. Instead of action there is further procrastination, there is further postponing. The government is doing nothing today to deal with the report or with the freight rate situation that it did not do a year ago or a couple of years ago. The government has no policy with regard to freight rates. It has a policy with regard to royal commissions. It has appointed as many as possible on as many subjects as possible. Get all the royal commission reports and in the main shelve them. Let them gather dust and procrastinate and postpone in the hope that the royal commission reports will be something of an answer for an electorate that is requiring action.
In his statement this morning the minister made it clear that this bill freezes only certain freight rates. It freezes the general class and commodity rates, but it does not freeze the competitive rates or the agreed charges. In other words it puts a ceiling on certain rates, and underneath the ceiling the rates can be adjusted upward right to the ceiling. So that while this measure does put some control on the revenues that may be obtained by the railway companies, it would be false to assume that it freezes railway revenue or even freight rates. It does not do this; it freezes only certain rates, and we certainly are in favour of any measure that prevents further horizontal increases.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this particular bill deals only with a certain restricted area of railway operations, and the railway companies are still free under the law, as they have been in the past, to undertake actions that have a very important effect on the freight users of this country.
The MacPherson royal commission report makes some submissions and recommendations with respect to passenger train service

on branch lines, to subsidies and to the Crows-nest rates. Nothing will be done with the Crowsnest rates. That is clear. But from all the information I can get the indications are that the discontinuance of passenger service will undoubtedly go forward, and the pressure that the railways have placed on the board of transport commissioners to allow them to abandon branch lines will be continued. I ask the minister whether he can give the house and the country any assurance whatsoever that there will be a freeze, or even a slow-down, in the rate at which the railway companies will seek to bring about an abandonment of railway passenger service or an abandonment of railway branch lines.
I come from a part of the country, and I suppose this is equally true of a majority of hon. members, where branch lines are exceedingly important. Over the years the people of Canada have felt that railway service was not something that could be confined or the jurisdiction over railway service was something that could not be confined, to private companies, but that the public interest demanded public control and a public policy for freight users in the country. The citizens of our nation who use branch line services are very much disturbed over the royal commission report which, under certain circumstances, would give the green light to a wholesale abandonment of branch lines in the country.
I say that the government is dealing with only part of the transportation problem; it is dealing with only one of the criticisms when it takes steps to prevent further increases in class and commodity rates. It is doing nothing constructive of which I am aware. I ask the minister to tell me what the government is doing, if it is doing something, to prevent the railways in our country getting from the board of transport commissioners the right to abandon all branch railway lines throughout the country.
I for one am going to resist, and resist for all I am worth, the wholesale abandonment of branch railway lines in Canada. The MacPherson report says that the railways could save $13 million annually by a wholesale abandonment of branch lines. I do not think the saving of $13 million by the railway companies warrants any kind of policy of wholesale abandonment of railway lines. Today the railways have a policy of wholesale abandonment of railway services. Usually the first thing they do is discontinue passenger train service. Then they put on mixed trains. A couple of years later they remove the passenger coach, and then they reduce the frequency of train service. Later they try to close the station and allow the agent to look

for other work. Then they amalgamate various sections of the railway for maintenance purposes.
This, Mr. Chairman, is almost a wholesale folding up and abandonment of railway services in our country. I say this has already gone so far that the government should develop at least an interim policy that would prevent its continuation until such time as an over-all, clear-cut railway policy is developed.
I have said that I am going to resist the discontinuance of branch line services in our country in any wholesale manner. I live in a community that has a branch line service. Ours is almost a branch off a branch, but although the service is only twice weekly it is important to that community. We do not want to see our costs of farming and of doing business skyrocket because of the tearing up of the railway track, thus condemning this small community, which is representative of hundreds of similar communities across the country, to economic death, the end of the community as it now is and a tremendous increase in the cost of doing business in the community.
The abandonment of railway lines is taking place. It is something that is with us. But if there is to be abandonment-and it may take place even though some of us oppose and resist it-I suggest that where it does take place the federal government should be prepared to put federal money and perhaps railway money into the building of paved highways over the right of way or along the right of way so that a community which loses its railway service will at least have an adequate highway system to replace the railway service.
As hon. members from western Canada know, many communities all over western Canada that have a very minimum of railway service also have very little by way of adequate highways serving them, and I say it would be a disgrace to our nation to tear up railway lines and leave these communities with inadequate highway facilities. I say it would be unjust, and it is not in keeping with a progressive nation that is looking forward to better and better services and a higher and higher standard of living.
The measure before the house is just a case of politically marking time as far as the government is concerned. It is a clear indication that the government has no policy, that the government has postponed and procrastinated. We can only hope that some day soon the government will develop an overall railway and transportation policy, that under this policy the freight service users of the country will be protected; that transportation facilities of all kinds will be integrated
Freight Rates Reduction Act in a fair and equitable manner and, most important of all, that the freight service users and the communities that depend on the railways will be given adequate consideration.

It seems to me that anyone who talks as though that kind of miracle could have been performed is not really talking realistically about this subject or making much of a contribution to the solution of a problem which I would say is one of the three or four most difficult problems that we have to solve in this country. It does seem to me that on the whole it would be a good thing for us in parliament to try to contribute to the solution of that problem, and surely the first point in its solution is to try to get the facts straight.
The Minister of Transport suggested in the course of his remarks yesterday that the present government had done very well because while there had been a 140 per cent increase under the former administration, there had only been a 17 per cent increase under the present administration.

speechtext:
I am not trying to distort the facts, but perhaps I could be allowed to put them in my own words. A 17 per cent increase was granted by the board of transport commissioners, and the government decided in 1959 and again in 1960 and is now asking parliament again to reduce that increase by a grant out of the treasury. That is what we are talking about. That is the purpose of this legislation. The increase was made, but the government decided that instead of the whole 17 per cent being paid by the shippers, or whoever does pay when it is charged in freight bills, approximately half of that increase should be paid by the taxpayers out of the treasury.
That is the point. But the government did not decide that it should not be paid. The government did not decide the railways were not entitled to it. The government decided that for the time being, whether or not the

railways were entitled to it, they should receive it. That was the decision announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he was acting prime minister in 1958. My hon. friend from Laurier placed that statement on Hansard yesterday.
If the railways are to provide services and if they are to pay, as we think they should, wages that are comparable with the wages paid to other workers in Canada for comparable work-and I do not see how, especially on a railway owned by the taxpayers, we could expect anything else-if those two conditions are to be met, these costs have to be paid by somebody. They have to be apportioned in some fashion, and the apportionment of them is really about all that parliament can do very much about. The question of how they are to be apportioned is admittedly a very complicated one.
Parliament decided years ago, after world war I, that the Crowsnest rates on grain were not to be changed; and no government and no political party, as the hon. member for Assiniboia quite properly said, has ever deviated from that position. It is true that in the report of the MacPherson commission it is recommended that the railways should receive, out of the treasury of Canada, some compensation for the maintenance of those rates. That will be, when the time comes, if it comes, if the government brings forward legislation, a very debatable question, but it is not under debate at the present time. The hon. member for Assiniboia, and my friend the hon. member for Laurier, and the Prime Minister at various times in the life of this parliament have made very clear the position on this question of all three parties represented in this house, and as far as I am aware there is no division at all on it.
After the Duncan commission made its report in 1927, if my memory is right, the government of that day saw fit to introduce the Maritime Freight Rates Act. That act had the effect of reducing, by means of compensation from the treasury to the railways the effect on shippers in the maritime provinces of certain freight rates. That legislation was extended to Newfoundland at the time Newfoundland became a part of Canada, in 1949.
In the year 1957 my hon. friend Mr. Harris brought a budget into this house, and in the course of that budget announced that the benefits to the shippers in the maritime provinces under the Maritime Freight Rates Act would be increased from 20 per cent to 30 per cent. That represented an increase of 50 per cent. It so happens that that was just the last of many steps taken by the Liberal government over the years following 1918 to mitigate the effect of the standard rates on certain sections of the community.

My friend the hon. member for Laurier did not mention that particular one because at the time of its introduction he was serving our country in another capacity.
That is really what the approach of the Liberal government has been, to mitigate for certain sections of the country the effect of the standard rates. Among the sections of the country that have benefited were the grain growers, the Atlantic provinces, the east-west traffic in respect of the bridge to which the hon. member for Laurier referred, and British Columbia because of the abolition of the mountain differential. By the various steps toward equalization that were taken by the board of transport commissioners as a result of the action taken in this parliament at the request of my friend the hon. member for Laurier in 1951, very considerable ameliorations have made more equitable to the Canadian people generally the weight of these charges.
Nobody can remove these charges without affecting revenues. Nobody can reduce them very materially, it seems to me, although automation may have some effect, as other kinds of efficiencies may also have, without reducing the services. I think it is foolish to pretend there is some magic way by which these can be changed. I know there are certain people who feel that if the whole system of control established by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when the board of railway commissioners was first established early in this century were abandoned; if free competition were permitted and the railways were allowed to set any kind of rates they liked, they might be able to be more efficient and cut their costs. Although I have a bias in favour of freedom, frankly I have a little scepticism about this particular argument. Nevertheless it is an argument that is made seriously by serious people.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

That is precisely what I intend to explain. I mean first of all, as I said before luncheon, that a certain measure of railway service, ever since confederation and prior to confederation-as one of the terms of confederation the Intercolonial railway was built-has been regarded as in the national interest; and that railway service must be paid for somehow by someone. There are two questions this parliament can settle and only two, it seems to me. The first is how much of that railway service really is in the national interest. The second is how that part of it which is in the national interest is to be paid for.
We in the Liberal party, when we were in office and since then, have never taken the view, any more than did the Turgeon commission, that horizontal increases or any other kind of increases in freight rates may not from time to time be necessary in order to pay for these services. We have never taken the view that there will not be certain instances in which some of the services should be paid for out of the treasury. In fact, as my hon. friend from Laurier pointed out earlier, it was the Liberal party that was responsible for the Maritime Freight Rates

Freight Rates Reduction Act Act, and it was the Liberal party that was responsible for the bridge in northern Ontario.
That was a decision that in the national interest the treasury should pay for these things instead of their being paid for by shippers or by whoever benefited directly from the service. We have decided twice already in this parliament, and we are now being asked to decide again as a stopgap, that half of a 17 per cent increase which the board of transport commissioners decided the railways were entitled to and the government agreed they were entitled to in 1958, or about half of it should be paid out of the treasury, and the other half should be paid by the shippers until such time as a long term solution is found.
We did not quarrel with that decision in 1959; we did not quarrel with it in 1960; and my hon. friend from Laurier indicated before luncheon, we do not quarrel with it now in itself. What we quarrel with is the fact that the government, instead of being straightforward about this matter; instead of saying that until the MacPherson commission had plenty of time to reach its conclusions that in the meantime they were going on with this stopgap; over and over again the government have held out false hopes about this matter and promises that were not fulfilled. For example, we have the Prime Minister in 1957 saying this. It is true he had no responsibility then, but in 1957, under what I called the other day that noontide of promises in that month of May four years ago, the Prime Minister had a few things to say about freight rates. At Drumheller he said there should be equalization of rail rates in Canada "within reasonable limits"-
I do not know what that means.
-to give a shot in the arm to agriculture and industry on the prairies... On freight rates he said that a rate pattern discriminatory to the west has been made worse by recent increases. This had struck "an almost paralysing blow" to industrial development in the west.
That is what the Prime Minister said. Then the Globe and Mail reported this:
He said a Conservative government would equalize freight rates as far as possible to help both agriculture and industry on the prairies compete with the rest of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this subject today. However, Your Honour will recall that this morning when the hon. member for Laurier was speaking in this house on the question of the equalization of freight rates for Canada, and in particular on the bill which is now before the house, I asked him whether he had ever said anything in reference to the Crowsnest pass freight rates and whether he had been reported as saying- because I recall the report-that the Crowsnest pass freight rates really were shackling the railways.
In order to make our position clear I think I should set out what I feel our position is as far as the Crowsnest pass freight rates are concerned. In doing so may I add these few introductory remarks. Over the years the fact is that we have enjoyed in western Canada, in the agricultural areas, the Crowsnest pass freight rates. They have assisted the farmers in getting their grain off the farms, into the markets and to Fort William at a reasonable freight rate.
That is why the Prime Minister has said on several, occasions during my short time as a member of parliament that the Crowsnest pass freight rates are really the economic magna carta for western Canada and in particular for the western farmers. In particular, when speaking on May 13, 1959, when the royal commission was set up to inquire into problems relating to the railways, the Prime Minister made very clear the stand of this government and the Conservative party as far as the Crowsnest pass freight rates were concerned. On Wednesday, May 13, 1959, as reported at page 3607 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said this:
When the Minister of Public Works as acting prime minister announced the government's intention to arrange for this review he assured the western farmers that such review would not mean that they would have to pay more freight on the shipment of grain for export. I wish to take this occasion to confirm this, in regard particularly to the action that may be taken as a result of the work of the royal commission. To make it clear beyond question, the Crowsnest pass rates are part of a bargain that was made between the railways and the government on the one hand and the settlers who went west on the other hand. We intend, in so far as this government is concerned, to see to it that that contract shaU not be broken.

Freight Rates Reduction Act Crowsnest pass freight rates. The Prime Minister also said on November 30, 1960, as reported at page 358 of Hansard-

In other words, we made it clear where this government and this party stand as far as the Crowsnest pass rates are concerned in relation to the shipment of western grain.

The Prime Minister made it plain when he dealt with the terms of reference of this commission that it was not to look into the Crowsnest freight rates because they were a solemn contract between the western sector, the western farmers, and the railways. It is also made clear that in consideration for that deal the railways got plenty. The Canadian Pacific Railway received land, and from that land they got petroleum, oil and natural gas; extremely valuable rights in the western provinces. It is true that since that date the C.P.R. has formed separate companies and turned those resources over to those companies; consequently they do not now show in the profits of the railway. Nevertheless, in considering this bill everyone from western Canada, irrespective of politics, knows, just as the hon. member for Assiniboia agreed with me this morning in reference to this subject, that as part of the deal the C.P.R. got that land and they got rich resources of petroleum, natural gas and other considerations.

From those country elevators the grain is loaded in cars in bulk. Anyone who has lived on the prairies from the time he was a boy has seen the trains, first steam and now diesels, taking the grain across the prairies. Those trains were half a mile or more long, and the cars were full of grain. I suggest that the manner in which this grain is transported makes that commodity easier for the railroads to handle than any other commodity in Canada. Surely this fact was behind the thinking of this government and of the Prime Minister, and that is why the solemn contract which was completed should stand on the statute books and the Crowsnest pass rates should not be interfered with. Surely this is why the subject was left out of the terms of reference of the royal commission.

The reason I ask this question is that in the friendly relations one has around the house, the talk behind the curtains and in the lobbies, one recognizes that there are a great many free enterprisers in the Conservative party. I see some of them in the house now. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome), the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) and the hon. member for York North (Mr. Cathers) would be among these free enterprisers. There is this group of people within the Conservative party who, as I know them, seem to stand for free enterprise. I know they welcome the Prime Minister's declaration. Yet again and again we keep getting this type of legislation which is nothing more than, perhaps not outright, crass socialism, but at least creeping socialism.
I should like to point out to the minister that the MacPherson commission took this view of the feeling in Canada today, and in the preface to the report said:
We sense in our hearings across the country an impatience and dissatisfaction with attempts to deal with the problem of transportation on a piecemeal or short run basis.
I think the commission really has got something. We have a call for a national transportation policy from the minister. In the light of the free enterprise ideal of the Prime Minister we must assume that this national transportation policy is going to be one of outright and open competition. We should like to know when we are going to see the C.B.C. being sold to private interests. When is the Canadian National going to be broken up and sold to private companies? What are we going to do with Polymer, Eldorado, Northern Transportation? Is this your election issue? This is what we would like to know, and we think the debate on second reading of this bill is another opportunity to call for information.
Now, the last point I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker, relates to the question of agreed charges. The minister knows that agreed


charges do not come within the framework of this bill. The minister also knows that every year the number of agreed charges increases. The revenue from agreed charges has been increasing and, in fact, there has been a marked increase in the two years since this bill went into effect. The assumption one has to make, therefore, since this subsidy is not going to affect agreed charges, is that agreed charges are spreading more widely and the subsidies should be making an increasing contribution to that portion of freight that does not fall within the agreed charges or other competitive rates. From this point of view one would assume that the subsidy required might be less, because if agreed charges are proliferating-and if hon. members check in the C.P.R. annual report they will see that the increase has been marked in that railway; and we know it has been marked in the C.N.R.-then there might be a possibility of reducing this subsidy; and I am trying to look at this matter from the point of view of someone with Conservative principles.
I should like the minister to be prepared, during the committee stage when we are going through the bill, to explain to us what effect the proliferation of agreed charges has had upon the fund and whether it is spreading out wider or more deeply in those freight areas where the agreed charges are taking the business away. I realize that is a rather clumsy explanation but I think the minister can see the point I am making. If agreed charges are increasing and are providing more and more revenue for the railway, then there is less and less need for this subsidy. We should like to know what the relationship has been in the two years' experience.
Perhaps the last thing I should say on this matter, Mr. Speaker, is this. I thought the review given by the hon. member for Laurier was a worth-while one to have on the record. However, I should like to suggest that to anyone who reads Hansard and follows it, it is a record as seen through Liberal party eyes. This is fine, but once you accept that qualification, you put some different interpretations upon the freight rate increases that took place and you put some different interpretations upon the actions of the board of transport commissioners. I thought it was a good review of the record from the Liberal point of view.
I should like to add that I myself can see little difference in attitude toward the freight rate question on the part of this government and on the part of the previous Liberal government. I am back at the only thing with which I started and it is this. We seem to have this new statement of principle on the part of the Prime Minister that he and the

Conservative party stand for free enterprise. I would therefore assume that this gives us a completely different approach. That is why I am back again wondering about those members in the house who support and stand with the Prime Minister for free enterprise, and wondering how they explain their vote and support for this particular measure.

Mr. Speaker, representing as I do a British Columbia constituency, I am very much pleased with this subsidy, even though the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said I am an out and out free enterpriser. This subsidy is not incompatible with free enterprise. This subsidy is based on giving to the western seaboard and the eastern seaboard equal advantages which are at present enjoyed by the central provinces because of the variety of services which are offered to them and the fact that they have competitive means of shipping apart from rail transportation.
I should like to refer to the submission made by the province of British Columbia to the royal commission on transportation in order to give to the house an idea as to how this matter affects British Columbia. On page 24 of the submission to which I referred, under the heading "British Columbia's Dependence on Rail", we find the following:
Shipments from British Columbia being bulky, heavy, and travelling long distances, are Ideally suited to rail and are in many cases tied to railways as there is no reasonably competitive form of transportation for these types of commodities.
Roads are difficult and costly to build through the province, and so trucks going to eastern Canada travel via the U.S.A. routes, paying license fees in each state. As there are no reciprocal licence arrangements between the province and the several states or provinces, truck operation over long hauls is very costly and impractical for the types of commodities which British Columbia has to offer.
As there is usually no alternative form of transportation, reasonable rail freight rates-reasonable in the light of costs of carriage-are absolutely essential for the economic health of British Columbia. The fact is that the province depends almost entirely on railway transportation for its welfare and the economic growth of the Province is in danger of becoming stunted by reason of high freight charges.
In a table on the following page is shown the distribution of traffic between transportation agencies with regard to incoming and outgoing shipments in the year 1957. It shows for rail shipments incoming, a figure of almost 13 million tons; for shipments outgoing, almost 11 million tons. As to other 90205-6-310
Freight Rates Reduction Act forms of transportation, you find for water a figure of 760,000 for incoming shipments and of 194,000 tons for outgoing shipments. With regard to highway shipment, you find a figure of 176,000 tons for incoming shipments and of 64,000 tons for outgoing shipments. Rail traffic therefore represents from about 90 per cent to 95 per cent of all traffic incoming and outgoing in British Columbia. Therefore the purpose of the bill is to prevent those areas which are entirely dependent upon rail-those captive areas-from taking the great percentage of any freight rate increases which the railroads need to have and must have. In order to prevent this from happening-a happening which would throttle the economic growth of the maritimes and of the west coast-I contend this subsidy is necessary and essential.
I should like to refer for a few minutes to another subsidy with which we do not agree. I refer to the so-called bridge subsidy. The bridge subsidy was recommended by the Turgeon commission on the basis of what they called an economic desert north of lake Superior. It was a subsidy to facilitate the movement of goods from eastern Canada to western Canada against the railhead north of lake Superior which, in the opinion of the commission was largely an unproductive area as far as freight is concerned.
In this same submission of the province of British Columbia there is a comparison between the number of tons of freight generated per mile of traffic in the bridge area between Sudbury and Port Arthur. It showed the number of tons per mile as 2,425. The Turgeon commission said that this area would not generate the traffic which could be generated in the prairie provinces. When you compare this figure of 2,425 tons with that in the province of Manitoba, all lines, and that in the province of Saskatchewan, you find that the number of tons per mile in the province of Manitoba is 1,698 and in the province of Saskatchewan the number of tons per mile is 1,121. This so-called unproductive area is therefore a great deal more productive of freight than are the prairie provinces per mile of track.
The location of this bridge north of lake Superior gives an economic advantage to shippers in eastern Canada who already have alternative forms of transportation not available to the west coast. This puts us at a disadvantage in shipping eastward across the bridge. In the opinion of the province of British Columbia the bridge subsidy unfairly discriminates against that province.
Mr. Speaker, I have one other point and I will have finished. In regard to the general subsidies recommended by the MacPherson

Freight Rates Reduction Act commission, and so on, in the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, April 18, in the business section there appeared an article written by Mr. John Meyer. He pointed out that these subsidies would not be of the magnitude envisaged in the report because for one thing a subsidy to the C.N.R. would simply reduce the deficit, and on the other hand a subsidy to the C.P.R., because the C.P.R. is already in a 50 per cent tax bracket, would mean that half the subsidy would be returned in the form of corporation taxes.
Hon. members from the prairie provinces have gone into the question of the Crowsnest pass rates. However, I should like to point out that the dissenting opinion in the first volume of the report of the MacPherson commission pointed out that there were many ways in which costs had been loaded against the grain shipper of the west and these rates were much closer to being compensatory than is generally believed. I would refer hon. members to that dissenting opinion in the report if they wish to obtain a much fairer idea as to the true effect of the Crowsnest pass rates.

rights established for the producer under a solemn compact, and no effort on the part of any hon. member to throw any doubt on that record will be successful.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to comment for a moment or two on some remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). The hon. member for Port Arthur seemed to think he was going to embarrass us in this party by referring to the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had said we were in favour of private enterprise. So we are, but we are also in favour of common sense.
A great leader of our party used a phrase of which I like to remind people again and again. I am referring to Mr. Meighen. He spoke about the "immortal grounds of common sense". I like to think that I belong to a party that tries to look at things in a common sense way. If we look at our society in a common sense way we know it is not pure private enterprise, free enterprise or public ownership; we have a mixture of these things in our economy.
I am quite ready to proclaim, on behalf of our party we have gone into certain aspects of public ownership because we thought it was practical, good business and common sense. I refer particularly to the hydroelectric in Ontario, which I suppose it is fair to say was instituted very largely by a Conservative government. It got under a full head of steam in the days of Sir James Whitney. I may also refer to the C.N.R. and Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in the days of the first world war. He had a great deal to do with the setting up of that railway.
We remember what happened. We remember there had been a rather extreme orgy of railroad building in Canada in the early years of the century. Both parties had a good deal to do with that, so honours are equal there. We were a bit too enthusiastic. In the days of the first war the situation grew acute, and I suppose Mr. Meighen was responsible more than anybody else for setting up the C.N.R. roughly in its present form. So when the hon. member for Port Arthur twits us and wants 90205-6-310i
Freight Rates Reduction Act to know what we stand for, I will say to him that we stand for common sense, and when we run into a situation of this kind when by reason of what has happened in the past- and the judgment of both parties enters into this-we have set up an organization-I refer to the Canadian National Railways-which has been loaded up, as we all know, by a lot of unprofitable lines and become a kind of basket into which everything was dumped. When such an operation encounters difficulties and is in need of assistance I make no apology for belonging to a party which comes along in a practical way and gives it assistance. It does not worry me if somebody says it is a form of grant and that we are subsidizing the railways. This is the situation we face, and I hope we shall always continue to face such situations in what I regard as a nondoctrinaire, practical, honest, straightforward way.

subtopic: AMENDMENT EXTENDING APPLICATION OF REVISED RATES
