We had a
discussion on this bill last evening and I think the position taken by those on this side of the house was made clear. However, we did have at least one extraordinary speech made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) and I should like to refer to some of the things which were said on that occasion before turning to another matter.
The hon. member for Vancouver South was highly excited last evening and I suppose one could excuse him for some of the things which were said. For instance, as reported at page 4848 of Hansard of May 15, he continued by saying this:
We were also treated to a dissertation by the hon. member for Laurier on how the Canadian National Railways was set up. It would be a free enterprise company which would operate outside of the control of the department. The minister would report to parliament on behalf of the company but would have nothing to say about its operations.
The hon. member continued to that effect. Well, one has only to read the statement which I made to become convinced that I made no such dissertation. I made a passing reference in one sentence to the position of the C.N.R. and that will be found at page 4843 of Hansard of the same date. This is what I said:
The minister likes to say in the House of Commons that he does not direct the affairs of the
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.)
Canadian National Railways but that it administers its own affairs, and that he represents it and reports on its behalf in the house.
That is a position which I think all hon. members will accept. It was not a dissertation. It was just a simple sentence in passing.
Then the hon. member for Vancouver South said:
We were told in the committee, coming back to the setting up of this company, that it was not for politicians or members of parliament to put their noses into the business of this company: that this was part of the function of the management and we were simply there to receive the report of the management on the way the railway had been operated.
I challenge that statement. I have no recollection of any member being told anything of the kind in that language during the proceedings of that committee. But what I have always been told, and what I have always respected when I sat on the other side of the house and, what I hope, the present minister would respect, is that there shall be no political interference with the management of the C.N.R. If that is what the hon. member for Vancouver South is seeking, namely, to have members of parliament interfere politically with the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, I say to him and to others of a like mind that that would be a sad day. The establishment-the board of directors and the administrative section of the C.N.R.-is there to administer the railways. There were days in Canadian history when there was political interference with the affairs of the railway. Those were sad days and I hope they will never occur again. When we were in office we repeatedly took the position in connection with the C.N.R. that the affairs of the railway were to be managed by the company and that there should be no political interference. Certainly, I have not heard it said that things should be otherwise, except in this statement of the hon. member last evening.
Then at page 4849, referring to myself, he said:
He talks about curtailing expenses on the part of the public; he says that the public are against curtailing C.N.R. expenses and by inference that means that the public desires that there should be a deficit on the part of the C.N.R. This is what it means. He means that the C.N.R. is not to be made a profitable, efficient operation.
Never, in any of my remarks have I either directly or indirectly inferred that that should be the case. If the hon. member will look at page 4844 of Hansard he will see that I said:
The deficits of Canadian National Railways this year is probably one of the highest in its history. The estimate given for 1961 is not too encouraging. What it will be I am unable to say but it will

certainly be substantial, and if the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation or part thereof are not implemented then, of course, the deficit will reach astronomical figures.
I made one other reference to the Canadian National Railways in that respect. A little earlier I said:
There has also been a fairly substantial reorganization of the various districts of Canadian National Railways recently. I am told this is in an effort to curtail expenditure, a move, incidentally, which is extremely unpopular with the men and with the public.
Then I said:
Notwithstanding that reorganization, it is still found necessary by the government to increase the board of directors.
Where is there any reference directly or indirectly in this statement, or any place else in what I said last night, that I favoured a higher deficit for the Canadian National?
Then, the hon. member got terribly exercised over the statement I made concerning regional representation. "Take the men where they are", he said. "Get good men, no matter where they come from". Look at the annual reports of the Canadian National Railways and see what the government has done. It has made regional appointments. All one has to do is to look at the annual reports of the Canadian National Railways to see that that policy which was established by the earlier administration was followed in 1957. There were seven directors in that year, two from Ontario, two from Quebec, two from the west and one from the Atlantic provinces. In 1958 two new appointments were made on the basis of the same regional representation. In 1959 again we had the same group of directors, two from Ontario, two from Quebec, one from the maritime provinces-

Mr. Speaker, I hope I am on the right spot now. After listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier I can probably get on to the subject which is the matter of increasing the board of directors from seven to 12; in other words, adding five extra directors. This brings back to my mind a time when there was a motion before the house having to do with lending the president of the Canadian National Railways to the government of Mexico for six months with the purpose in mind of rehabilitating the railway of that country. I recall that the then member for Toronto Northwest (Tom Church), who afterwards became the member for Broadview, was heartily in favour of it. In fact, he was going to support the motion. The president at that time was Sir Henry Thornton, for whom he did not have a very high regard. It was suggested that the motion would apply first for only six months, but he suggested that it be 365 days for next year and for five years hence and put the motion through as a local improvement.
The legislation before us has to do with increasing the membership of the board. The hon. member for Laurier says that he does not see any reason why the membership should be increased because we have a great deal of unemployment. I would say there are good reasons for increasing the membership of the board. We should have more people on the board, but they should not be there from the regional point of view; they should not

Canadian National Railways Act be on the board for the reason suggested by the hon. member for Port Arthur, namely that it would add prestige. We should get men of business renown who would help to increase the business of the railway. The hon. member for Greenwood made the same statement and I think it is quite reasonable.
The board of directors should consist of practical men who know how to run the railways and would run them as the president did in the days when Tommy Church was the member for Broadview. The president at that time was a railway man and had great experience in the first war. He made a fairly good job of running the railroad. In fact, he was very popular with the railroad men because he made a real good job of public relations. He was highly admired by the men. The same cannot be said of the president of the Canadian National Railways at the present time.
I have said in the past in this house that I am not an idolater of the president of the Canadian National Railways, nor am I enamoured of the work he has done as president of that organization. I have repeatedly said that to my way of thinking he is not the proper man in the right place, and this is the time to discuss it. I have repeatedly made remarks along this line and I have found out one thing. It seems to me there is a coterie of members in this house who seem to regard him very highly. If you make any remarks about him with which they do not agree they assume right away that it is almost treasonable. They start to go after you. This is the way I see it. If you gore or goad one of their sacred oxen they immediately put you down as looking for the job. One thing is certain. I am not looking for the job. I have no inclination that way. I have no intention of seeking it. I do not suppose anyone in this house would care for the job under the conditions under which it is operated at the present time.
However, now that we are taking steps to increase the board of directors I presume it is being done for the purpose of improving the board. When I first read the bill I thought that here was an operation like that which Tommy Church tried to carry out in order to get rid of the president at that time. I thought that this would be a good opportunity to dispose of the president of Canadian National Railways, not becaus'e we want to do him any particular harm but because he has appeared before committees of this house and not only has defied them but has told them that if they were not satisfied with his services they should get rid of him because he did not want to be there and we should oblige him.

There are enough people throughout the country who are not satisfied with his services, particularly those who are working for Canadian National Railways. I have had many of them write to me and call me on the telephone and having sorted out the ones you would not pay attention to from those putting forward genuine criticisms and offering suggestions for improvement but who do not want to have their names mentioned I would say this is the time to discuss the matter of what you are going to do with the board and whom you are going to appoint. Mr. Speaker, I would say that from the point of view of economics and saving money the advice of the house in regard to the selection of directors is very appropriate. When you are sizing up the directors you are going to appoint you have to bear in mind that some of them are in receipt of exceptionally high salaries and by removing the one who is receiving the highest salary of all you could then appoint others at lower salaries and make a great saving there while at the same time there would be a vast improvement. You could appoint the kind of directors who would be more acceptable to the people of Canada to run the railway.
The matter of free enterprise has been discussed. The only free enterprise I can see is that when a train comes into the Ottawa and Toronto stations the passengers are dumped off with the freight and the only freedom the passengers have is the freedom to walk a long distance while the freight is carried away by truck. Perhaps I might put the matter this way. A farmer was taking a load of manure to his friend's place about ten miles up the road and a hobo stopped him and asked him for a lift. The hobo went to get in with the farmer but the farmer told him to get on the back on top of the load of manure. As the farmer was going up the road a friend stopped him and said, "What have you got there"? He said "I have a load of manure and a hobo". A little farther along he was asked the same question. He was asked the same question four or five times and he replied, "I have a load of manure and a hobo". Finally another friend of his came along and was about to ask the same question when the hobo said to the farmer, "The next time when you are asked what you have would you mind giving me the preference"? All I am asking is that the passengers at least get the preference when they arrive at the station. This is the kind of deal the president has been giving the passengers in the past and it does not go over very well.
I can also remember when the railway was first started. I believe D. B. Hanna was the president at the time. I can remember a speaker waxing eloquent on the platform

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length on this legislation because I promised the minister I would be brief. Besides, I wonder why this piece of legislation is being submitted. I have been sitting here for 21 years, and frankly, I have never seen such an insignificant and useless bill.
When I got here last evening, I read the remarks made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) when he introduced this legislation, and I noted that he did no more than outline the historical background of the C.N.R. board of directors, and to say how many members there were on the board of directors of other railway companies. I tried to find a single argument that might cause the members of this house to support this legislation, but found nothing that might

Canadian National Railways Act justify an increase from seven to 12 in the number of board directors, except perhaps that such a change might provide, as the minister said, a better geographical representation in the C.N.R. management.
In my opinion, the remarks of the minister indicate that neither he nor the former minister of transport are convinced of the necessity and the usefulness of that change.
It is not my intention to repeat the arguments put forward yesterday and this afternoon by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), because he clearly set out our party's stand. As the minister knows, however, this railway matter is of particular interest to me because there are several hundred people in my riding who are employees of the C.N.R.
I had an opportunity, during the budget debate in January, to make certain suggestions which I feel would have produced more significant results both for the railway company and for its employees. The minister knows from experience that the mere fact of increasing from seven to 12 the membership of the board of directors of this crown company will in no way reduce the deficit, or the number of lay-offs.
I am still wondering why a measure such as this is being introduced at the end of the session, when we have so many serious problems to deal with. I wonder whether the Conservative government still has friends with nothing to do and whether appointments must be made in order to satisfy those friends. Well, under the circumstances I do not think that the house should be called upon to adopt such a bill. In my opinion, one way of providing this company with the assistance it needs would be to endow the C.N.R. research division with the required sum of money so that a solution may be found to the problems now facing it.
The minister should now know, after discussing the point with the company's high officials that automation and the new technological developments have created problems that must be urgently met if we want the C.N.R., which is now in a bad situation, to continue its operations. The necessary answers to those problems must be found.
There is another matter which looks as important to me. I do not know whether the minister ever had the opportunity of meeting railway employees, but certainly he must have realized that the morale of the C.N.R.'s 70,000 to 75,000 employees is at a very low ebb.

Mr. Chairman, those workers, who have been with the railway for 10, 15, 20 or 25 years or even more, have been living in uncertainty in recent years. They are worried about the future.
I hope the minister will confer with the C.N.R. authorities and discuss the matter with them.
I do not want to speak at length on this matter today, because I know that the minister has to leave soon. I hope, however, to take up this subject again when his estimates are before the house.
Once again, for the reasons set forth by the hon. member for Laurier, and for the few reasons I have mentioned myself, I suggest that this bill is altogether useless. The $35,000, $40,000 or $50,000 that we shall spend on salaries for these new directors could certainly have been put to better use.
I see the minister is shaking his head. Yet he knows very well that the issues now confronting the C.N.R. will not be settled by the appointment of those five new directors.
When making his statement, the minister did not justify this legislation on any valid ground.
Mr. Chairman, this is a far cry from the promises made by members now sitting on government benches. I remember, for instance, that before 1957, the former minister of transport always rose in immediate protest whenever there had been any dismissals.
Well, Mr. Chairman, for the last three years, the minister, when asked what he intends to do about those dismissals, always answers: This is not my business, but the responsibility of the railway management.
Mr. Chairman, the only legislation devised to help our national railways at this time, is this appointment of five new directors.
You may be assured that I am not prepared to endorse this legislation; to me it is completely futile. It can only increase government expenditures without bringing in anything in return.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, I shall vote against the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to use much of the time of this house, but because of the present position of the C.N.R. and the government's decision to introduce legislation to increase the number of its directors from seven to 12, I must say a few words.
This increase in the number of board members, believe me, Mr. Chairman, will not remedy the ills of the C.N.R.
In my opinion, it is of minor importance that we should have seven, 12 or 20 directors. The important thing is to see that the management is improved.
Canadian National Railways Act
I am one of those who thinks that railway management, not only the C.N.R. but also the C.P.R., has been pitiful for many years.
First of all, they allowed a very important field of operations to fall into the hands of other organizations without thinking of developing it themselves.
I recall that in 1936, talking to one of the C.P.R.'s vice chairmen, I pointed out that his company was losing its secondary line services to bus companies, and its freight traffic to highway transport companies because his company had not seen fit to develop those services itself.
Do you know what the company's vice chairman replied to me, in 1936? He said:
(Text):
It is only a passing fancy.
(Translation):
Well, this "passing fancy" is the cause of the present loss of revenues of our railways.
Therefore, no matter how many or few directors we have on the C.N.R., this legislation will not bring any significant change.
We know that when it comes to choosing directors, a private company like the C.P.R., for instance, will pick men who are financially interested, who are interested in getting dividends.
It may go and get the president or general manager of General Motors or Ford Motors, which make a very wide use of railways and other means of transportation for their cars; and other big manufacturers who may also be interested. But in the case of the C.N.R., those directors merely become civil servants like the others; they are getting no particular benefits, except seeing their names prominently displayed in government reports.
Well, I do not think this is enough. First of all, the C.N.R. services have to be improved.
In December, I travelled to Boston, and I must tell you I have never seen such poor service as the one between Montreal and Boston via the C.N.R. Frankly, it was disgusting, and I understand why people prefer a longer trip via some other line rather than go there via the C.N.R.
Let us therefore start by improving what we already have. As I said just now the number of directors is not so important. I do think, as the hon. member for Levis said a moment ago, that this legislation is more intended to create soft berths for party supporters as was done, incidentally, for the

Canadian National Railways Act defeated candidate in Russell who was given a very important position just to keep him out of the way at the next general election.
If this is how it is proposed to improve the C.N.R., it is a mistake. The number of directors is not important, I repeat, but, as the hon. member for Levis said, if that money were offered to the research department of the C.N.R. to determine the cause of the evil, C.N.R. officials could take the necessary steps to improve the situation, and that would be practical and serious. It would be much wiser than to increase the number of board directors from seven to 12, which I consider useless, because they are merely civil servants having no authority to work, with parliament always keeping an eye on them, something they do not like at all.
If they could get something out of it, like directors of the C.P.R., who are shareholders and who receive dividends, we could then hope that 10, 12 or even 20 directors would improve the situation.
But what good will result from adding new directors who have no particular interest in the company? I think this would entail a useless expense which will bring no profit, but rather an additional deficit, to the C.N.R., and that will not help the railway workers either.
These last few years, the company appointed many superintendents and, at the same time, has cut down substantially on the number of its employees. This service should be reorganized, for not only is the public questioning the efficiency of the C.N.R. management but employees too no longer have confidence in the management. You might claim that some of the directors were appointed under a Liberal government. That is not the point. When there is something bad somewhere, I am not afraid to say so and even to admit as much. I say there is something wrong in that field, and it is not by increasing the number of directors that we are going to set things straight. It is a matter of finding the appropriate means of improving the whole system of transport in all its forms. I for one would say that the best way would be to provide the research department with more money, so that it can seek a way out of the present difficulties, and not to appoint 12 directors as suggested by the minister.

Mr. Speaker, before I answer some of the statements made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) I should like to say this to the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) who stated so emphatically that he tried to find one argument for increasing the number of directors but could not find one valid one. If he would compare the operating statements of the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. over the past few years, he might find a few arguments. He might find an argument in the fact that the C.N.R. deficits over 1960 and 1959 were $110 million which were paid for by the taxpayers whereas in the same two years the C.P.R. contributed $53 million in the form of corporation tax payments. If you have a business operation and are not too successful and if you have very successful competitors, the wise businessman takes a look at the practice of his competitors and is not afraid to copy any of the practices which he feels may be of advantage to him.
Turning to the hon. member for Laurier, may I say that there are several matters I wish to discuss with him. I should like to quote from page 4844 of Hansard with regard to what he had to say about representation geographically on the board of directors. This is the way in which he starts out:
There is, of course, another very serious matter to which consideration must be given and that is territorial representation. That question is inevitably going to arise if the directorship is increased. This question is going to arise if the number of directors is such that there is likely to be more than one representative for each province, and that is, of course, what is going to happen here. Twelve directors will mean that there will be more than one director for each province. When there is one director from each province it seems to me that unquestionably there is a solemn duty to represent the interest of that province without, of course, neglecting the national interest. If there are two from a province you may well find that sectional divisions will arise.
Then the hon. member goes on to say this:
Then there is the question of the representation of the province of Quebec if there are 12 directors. With 12 directors it will be expected that the province of Quebec will be accorded equitable representation having regard to its population. If it does not get such representation I need hardly tell the minister that he will hear about it in due course because he has repeatedly stated that the C.N.R. was not fair and just to his province. I am not going to put on the record the statement he has made. I have used it before and I do not think this is the opportune time to repeat it.
Then the hon. member goes on to say in the next paragraph:
It seems to me that the directors ought to be appointed from the point of view of their competence rather than from the point of view of geographical and political interests.
You get these statements coming from both sides of the mouth of the hon. member for

Laurier. If he wishes to quote his espousal of the interests of the provinces, he has one paragraph. If he wishes to say what a broadminded gentleman he is, looking only for the best men to do the best job, he has another paragraph. All through this speech we can find this double talk. The hon. member can see that this is so, if he looks at the record.
The hon. member accused me of wanting narrow, regional representation, whereas my plea was for broad, regional representation very much along the lines that we have at the present time. However, I think we should have a larger representation from Ontario and Quebec simply because those directors could get together more often and more easily, and this board of directors must be a functioning and working board.
Then the hon. member for Laurier suggested that I was advocating political interference. He quoted from page 4848 of Hansard to substantiate that charge. This is just as much misrepresentation on his part as he accused me of last night.
We were told in the committee, coming back to the setting up of this company, that it was not for politicians or members of parliament to put their noses into the business of this company, that this was part of the function of the management and we were simply there to receive the report of the management on the way the railway had been operated.
The hon. member for Laurier says this means I want political interference. For the hon. member's information, it means that I want the sessional committee to have the power to get straight answers to questions put by members of the committee, rather than having the president of the company hiding behind the fact that this information is not in the public interest, or it is before a royal commission, or any of the numberless excuses we were given in place of the information we sought.
This paragraph has to do with the securing of information from the railroad when its representatives are appearing before the committee. The hon. member was not of too much assistance in trying to dig out this information.

The hon. member recalled to Mr. Gordon how the C.N.R. had been set up and how it

Canadian National Railways Act inference that the hon. member wanted larger and larger expenditures and therefore larger and larger deficits. I do not understand how the hon. member for Laurier can say that I misrepresented what he said, because it is clear, although in the typical fashion of the hon. member for Laurier he leaves himself a bolt-hole in the next paragraph, in the same manner as he did with regard to the other question.
I should like to put on record a few comparisons. The hon. member for Laurier says there is no point in making comparisons with the C.P.R. because the C.N.R. is a crown company. The fact that they are both railroads and are both engaged in almost identical operations does not seem to have any bearing on the matter. The hon. member felt that the C.N.R., because its number of employees had been reduced, did not need additional directors in order to increase efficiency or improve over-all management. In fact, the inference was-although this was not said-that because the number of employees had been reduced, therefore the number of directors might well be reduced.
There is a chart in the annual report of the C.N.R. which gives the figure of employees of all services. One has to interpolate on this chart, Mr. Speaker, because these figures are not exact. However, the number of employees in all services of the C.N.R. is 97,000; for the C.P.R. the figure is 74,000. The mileage operated by the C.N.R. is 26,000, and for the C.P.R. it is 17,000. The number of directors for the C.N.R. is seven, and for the C.P.R. it is 24. But the C.N.R. has a very fine record in regard to the number of vice presidents. They certainly come up well there, because they have 17 vice presidents as compared with 12 on the C.P.R.
The total number of officers in the C.N.R. is very fine too. They may not have many directors, but they have 28 officers on the C.N.R. as compared with 19 on the C.P.R. I also wish to put on record the deficit position of the C.N.R. and the surplus position of the C.P.R.
All these things would, I think, lead any reasonable person to assume that there is something wrong with the operation of the C.N.R. I should like to make one suggestion to the minister, and it is not referred to in this bill I would ask the minister to ensure that, by regulation or however it may be done, the executive committee of the C.N.R. become a functioning committee and a real executive committee.
I say this because at the present time the executive committee of the C.N.R. consists of


two directors and the president. They meet monthly, as I understand it, in order to ratify the acts of the president. However, it is not necessary that the same two directors be picked by the president each month to ratify his actions. The president may pick any director any month. The executive committee is not set up as a working committee of the board of directors, or so I have been given to understand following questions asked in the sessional committee. The president appoints the executive committee, and that is the point I was trying to make when I said the C.N.R., set up to have all the advantages of free enterprise, operates with none of the disadvantages. It is impossible to call the head of the railroad to account for the operation of the affairs of the railroad. That accounting is made to a hand picked group appointed by the president himself to ratify his actions, and this is the so-called executive committee.
If we refer to the C.P.R.-and I think it might be well to follow the lines of a successful operation-we find that the executive committee consists of seven directors who are named in the annual statement. It is they who ratify the acts and the decisions of the officers of the company. This makes sense. The other system under which the C.N.R. is operating certainly does not make sense. I do not know whether this should be written into the bill or how it would be undertaken, but I certainly believe that something should be done to set up a proper, functioning executive committee of the board of directors.
I think I have now made the contribution which I set out to make to this debate. I believe this is a good measure, and I am sure that hon. gentleman on the other side also believe it is a good measure. In my opinion it will do much to restore the confidence of the public and the confidence of many individual members of parliament in the operations of the C.N.R.

Mr. Chairman, Bill No. S-12 provides for an amendment to the act of incorporation of the Co-operative Life Insurance Company with head office in Regina, Saskatchewan.
Perhaps I can give the committee a brief history of its passage through the other place. First reading was given in the other place on February 9 and second reading on February 15. It was considered by the banking and commerce committee of the other place and reported without amendment on March 22, 1961. It passed third reading the next day. There are only two proposed changes and these are being made for the purpose of assuring policyholder members throughout Canada that control of the company will not be centralized in Saskatchewan and in particular at head office.
It might be of some interest and in order to give a brief outline of the history of the company. The Co-Operative Life Insurance Company was originally incorporated in 1945 as a co-operative company under the co-operative section of the Saskatchewan insurance act and almost immediately thereafter commenced to sell life insurance. In 1946 a petition was submitted to the government in Ottawa to obtain a dominion charter. The Co-Operative Life has operated since 1947-

In effect, under clause 1 precautions are written into the act to prevent employees of the company from exercising proxies of other policyholders and thus to prevent the control

Private Bills
of the company from falling into the hands of head office personnel. I think this is very clearly set out in the new section 4 (1) under clause 1 of the bill. Clause 2 of the bill would add a new section 4A to the above-mentioned statute. Its purpose is to prevent the control of the company from being concentrated in any one designated region. This will bring control of the operations of the company in line with a procedure that is followed by most of the co-operatives in western Canada, namely, the procedure of delegate voting. Delegates will be elected annually from each of the six electoral districts set up as follows: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and the Atlantic provinces including Newfoundland.
Bill No. S-12 was considered at a meeting of the standing committee of banking and commerce of the house on April 19. At that committee meeting the superintendent of insurance indicated that he was not opposed to the proposed changes. As you will note from today's Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day, the house's standing committee on banking and commerce made one slight amendment and that is noted on page 11 of Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day by the words "as amended''. Perhaps I might be allowed to outline this brief amendment. The new section 4A, clause 2 of the bill, reads as follows:
(1)	Each director shall be elected from a designated region in Canada and, to remain qualified, shall during office be ordinarily resident in such region: Provided-

-that at least one director shall be elected from each designated region and-

That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1952, to increase the monthly rates of allowances and permissible income ceilings; to allow for further exemptions in property and income; to modify certain conditions of service eligibility; to allow for administrative and organizational changes within the board and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the house rose last night I was making a few remarks with regard to this resolution.

Since I had only about five minutes available there was no chance to deal elaborately with the resolution; consequently I may find it necessary to recapitulate some of the things I said last evening. In the first place I will have to suggest a correction in Hansard at page 4868. In concluding my remarks I am reported to have said:
I do not know of any piece of legislation apart from the Disabled Persons Act which is more acceptable to veterans across Canada.
What I meant to say was, "apart from the Pension Act for disabled pensioners".
The Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act, with which we are now dealing, are the two basic acts which have been placed on the statute books for the assistance of veterans who have fought in Canada's wars.
Of the two acts some people feel that the War Veterans Allowance Act is the better. Others rely on the Pensions Act. I make no choice between the two; I think they are both very valuable. Over the years both have been amended from time to time to bring them up to date in relation to the experience gained in dealing with veterans of the wars.
Our first pension legislation goes back to the time of the Fenian raids and to 1885, after the Northwest Rebellion; but it was not until the conclusion of world war I, in fact not until 1930, that legislation was placed on the statute books dealing with the veteran who was not disabled by wounds. Over the years, from the conclusion of world war I until 1930, veterans organizations across the country, members of parliament of that day and other interested persons kept drawing public attention to the need of the unwounded veteran. Resolutions of committees were put forward, debates were held in the House of Commons and finally in 1930 the government of the day introduced a resolution, followed by a bill which, after consideration by a committee of the House of Commons and with amendments proposed thereto, came back, was passed and became the War Veterans Allowance Act.
It is rather interesting to look back at the debates of 1930 to see the reasons for introducing this type of resolution. If hon. members will examine Hansard for March 4, 1930, when the resolution was discussed, they will see that it was introduced by the Hon. J. H. King, who was minister of pensions and national health. In those days he was responsible for veterans' problems. The resolution that he brought before the house read as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances to war veterans, to provide assistance for certain veterans who are not in receipt of pensions, or who, if in receipt of pensions, are only partially pensionable, or who

are unemployable, and to provide for the administration, amounts, terms and conditions of such allowances, and for the payment of such sums as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the proposed legislation.
After a lengthy debate on the resolution stage and again on second reading the act was put on the statute books but from time to time it has had to be amended and now in 1961, 31 years later, we are suggesting still further amendments to this very valuable act. The basis on which the Hon. J. H. King placed his argument ran somewhat as follows, and I will quote some of his remarks just to give the committee an idea of what was in the minds of the government and members of parliament at that time. Mr. King said, as found at page 248 of Hansard of March 4, 1930:
Mr. Speaker, this will constitute an endeavour on the part of the government to meet an outstanding need in the lives of our veterans, which need has been recognized for some years but not provided for up to the present. I might direct the attention of the committee to the fact that in 1928 the committee on pensions and soldier problems included the following in their return to this house.
These were the committee's suggestions:
Your committee finds that one of the most serious situations confronting the department and the country generally is that relating to the employment and care of ex-members of the forces suffering from disability, broken down or burned out. A number of suggestions have been made to your committee for dealing with such cases. The committee recommends information be gathered which will be of assistance in framing the government's policy. The committee consider this the most serious problem which has arisen in connection with our ex-soldiers.
Then the Hon. J. H. King continued:
Our present pension legislation is specifically designed to compensate veterans whose disabilities are traceable to war service, but it has become increasingly apparent that some provision inevitably must be made to provide for the aged and unemployable veteran whose condition may not be directly traceable, under our present legislation, to war service.
Then he concluded his remarks with this passage:
The legislation which will follow this resolution is the most far-reaching of all veteran legislation so far introduced, in that, for the first time, it recognizes and makes provision for the man who was discharged fit, who is now unemployable, but who has not been found, under our present legislation, to be entitled to pension. In making provision for the non-pensionable man, Canada will be a pioneer in enacting legislation of this character. It will be seen that we propose to pay an allowance to men with front line service, or to pensioners, or former pensioners, no matter where their service, at a stated age, provided they are in necessitous circumstances. It is provided also to pay this allowance to men in this class, irrespective of their age, if they are found to be in necessitous circumstances and permanently unemployable. Reservations have been made as in
War Veterans Allowance Act
the old age pension legislation, restricting the amount receivable from this legislation and other sources combined.
It is not necessary for me to repeat what has been so frequently stated in this house, namely, that many men who rendered splendid service at the front are in need, and have been found nonpensionable. It is equally unnecessary for me to state that the effects of front line service have had a telling effect on the constitution and work expectancy of our veterans, so that many have aged before their time. This legislation provides for an allowance to these men. There is no doubt that in some cases the legislation will benefit men whose physical conditions are not due to their war service, but if we are to err we prefer to do so on the side of generosity toward those who served Canada so generously in their better days.
That, Mr. Chairman, represents the opinion of members of the House of Commons of the year 1930 because others who participated in the debate agreed with the summary presented by the minister at that time and added observations of their own. The experience of the country was that adequate arrangements had not been made through the Pension Act for veterans who had suffered from long service and who had no particular marks or physical disability to show for that service. Yet as the years went by and as the veterans became older the experience they had serving in the trenches began to tell upon them and they suffered accordingly.
The War Veterans Allowance Act established in 1930 has provided over the years for quite a number of individuals. Just to repeat one paragraph that I used last night, may I summarize the matter this way, that during the 30 years the act has been in operation 158,867 veterans and 28,075 widows and orphans have been given assistance and at the present time there are 47,204 veterans on the role and 19,266 dependents. That gives an indication, Mr. Chairman, of the number of people who have benefited from the act over the 30-year period I have mentioned. I have used figures which are shown in the annual report of the department for the fiscal year 1959-1960.
At the commencement of the legislation in the fiscal year 1930-31 there were only 2,219 veterans who came under the War Veterans Allowance Act and benefited therefrom. It was during the later thirties that the number steadily increased and it did not reach the peak, of course, until quite recently due to the fact that the veterans of the first world war are now of an average age of 70 years and a great many of them have reached the stage where they are not able to find employment and they have had recourse to this very valuable piece of legislation.
The act provides for seven classes of people, primarily veterans, of course, but also dependents. They can be considered in seven groups. The first is those who have survived

War Veterans Allowance Act from world war I or the South African war and a few dependents from the Northwest field force of 1885. The veterans there, not dependents, number 33,524. The second group of veterans comprises those from world war II and those who served with the special force in Korea. They number 6,676. Then there is a third class who served in both world war I and world war II, 992 of whom are assisted under this act. Provision has been made for veterans who served with commonwealth and allied forces and who are resident in Canada, 6,012 in number, or a grand total of veterans in these five classes of 47,204. Then, you have two additional classes, widows, who number 19,016, and orphans, who number 250. These veterans are found right across Canada in every province. I have a table here indicating that distribution. I think it is of interest to the committee to have some of this background material placed on the record at this stage. As other members participate in the debate, I hope they will add their observations with regard to the value of the War Veterans Allowance Act and also make their suggestions with regard to areas in which this act may be improved.
Subsequently, if the resolution passes and the bill passes second reading, we will refer the bill to the standing committee on veterans affairs for their detailed study and suggestions. I am sure we are all of the same opinion as the members of the house were in 1930, that this is a non-partisan operation in which we are working solely for the benefit of the veterans of Canada.
The distribution by provinces of the veterans and their dependents who come under the War Veterans Allowance Act is as follows: Newfoundland, 1,540; Prince Edward Island, 858; Nova Scotia, 4,650; New Brunswick, 3,199; Quebec, 7,572; Ontario, 24,316; Manitoba, 5,192; Saskatchewan, 3,015; Alberta, 4,634; British Columbia, 12,707. Each province has its quota of veterans under the War Veterans Allowance Act and in each province the Department of Veterans Affairs has an office operating to give care and attention to these veterans.
In addition, of course, there is the hospital service which is available to our veterans, not only those disability pensioners who are suffering from their wounds but also the veterans who are under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Just in passing, I might mention the fact that there are 11 veterans' hospitals located across Canada in Halifax, Lancaster, Ste. Foy, Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Montreal, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver, Victoria and, in addition, there are special wings in certain civic hospitals, veterans homes and health and occupational centres. The bed

capacity in the hospitals is 8,450. Patients are admitted at the rate of about 50,000 per year, and some of that number would be people about whom I am talking tonight, people under war veterans allowance.
I referred earlier to the financial obligation that has been incurred. I will not give the 'figures over the years, but in 1955 the financial obligation was approximately $27 million. As a result of changes which have occurred in the act since that time and the increase in the number on war veterans allowance, the financial obligation rose in the fiscal year 1956-57 to $41 million and last year stood at $57 million. The proposal that we are bringing before the house today will increase the financial obligation. In so far as the veterans of earlier wars are concerned, it is a decreasing obligation each year because veterans of the South African war are now in their eighties and some in their nineties. The veterans of the first world war have not a great life expectancy and, as the records indicate, they are passing off our books at the rate of 3,000 per year.

speechtext:
I hope that the hon. member for Kootenay West continues to persevere and last in this house for a very long time, so long as his constituents think it is advisable he should do so.
There is one problem that has given us concern. It is the fact that during February and March we dealt with amendments to the Pension Act for disability pensioners and we raised pensions by 20 per cent across the board, with 33-J per cent for orphan children who had not been included in an earlier increase. On consideration of the problem, it seemed wise to deal with the War Veterans Allowance Act in the same session if at all possible. The reason is that there are approximately 13,000 disability pensioners who are in the lower brackets, 5 per cent, 10 per cent and 15 per cent, who are also war veterans allowance recipients. Having increased the rates under the Pension Act I knew immediately that was done some pensioners would feel that they had not received much of an increase because if they were on war veterans allowance, the amount of the increase in the pension was correspondingly deducted from the war veterans allowance. In so far as the approximately 13,000 disability pensioners who are on war veterans allowance are concerned, therefore, no increase has resulted. If in a year that the Pension Act is amended the War Veterans Allowance Act is also amended, then both classes of veterans are looked after

and those who are under both acts are certainly given what is intended in the way of increases.
Although the amendment to this act was not forecast in the speech from the throne, it has been possible to bring it forward this session. I am sure that before very long the house will be able to deal fully with the measure and make it possible to pay to the people on war veterans allowance the increases that seem advisable.
The resolution before you, Mr. Chairman, suggests that the measure which will later be brought before the house will result in an increase in the monthly rates of allowances and permissible income ceilings; that it will allow for further exemptions in property and income; that it will modify certain conditions of service eligibility and will make provision for certain administrative and organizational changes within the board. That is the nature of the proposal which we are bringing forward.
Our hope is that these amendments will improve the War Veterans Allowance Act. These amendments will give an increase of income to people on war veterans allowance, will raise the permissible income ceiling, and generally will bring it up to date having regard to present difficulties and living standards. Although I do not think anyone is prepared to state that the war veterans allowance rates are adequate for all the needs of those who are under this act, nevertheless this is in keeping with what has been done in the past. There has been a steady rise in the rates. Then there are these other benefits, such as the hospitalization benefit, which are of considerable advantage to people on war veterans allowance.

I think I have perhaps now said enough to indicate to the committee that we treat this War Veterans Allowance Act with the greatest seriousness. It is an important piece of legislation. It came about through joint effort in 1930, preceded by representations from both sides of the house of that day and by representations made over the years by veterans organizations. The Canadian Legion and all other veterans organizations have given close attention to the War Veterans Allowance Act.

War Veterans Allowance Act At their annual meetings they have put forward resolutions suggesting changes for the better in the War Veterans Allowance Act and from time to time those changes have been incorporated into legislation which has been placed on the statute books. I feel sure that the veterans organizations will continue to make suggestions to us.
As I visit Legion branches and veterans groups I am impressed with the interest which the younger veterans-I refer to the veterans of the second world war and of Korea-show in the care and attention that is being given to the older veterans. Many a younger veteran has spoken to me of his pleasure at the increase in the Pension Act which we made early this spring and his interest in the proposal now on the order paper with regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act. The younger veteran wants to see the older veteran looked after. There is of course a community of interest among veterans. The younger veteran knows that his experiences in wartime were not any more severe than were those of the men who served in South Africa or the first world war; and he, recognizing that fact, wants the older veteran to be looked after. I hope that we can achieve that objective.
As far as the South African veterans are concerned, for example, I hope that not one of those men will suffer in his declining years through any lack of attention on the part of the House of Commons. If there is any field in which we have been negligent in assisting veterans of that period, let us correct the situation. The same thing applies with regard to first world war veterans. Men who have served their country well, who have suffered and who have not had the opportunities after the first world war to establish themselves as satisfactorily as they might have done, through no fault of their own, are the men whom a grateful country should assist. Let us not forget that the first world war veterans, after being demobilized, did not have the privileges which accrued to the second world war veterans in 1945 and subsequent years. The plans had not yet been laid. The country was inexperienced in dealing with a large number of veterans. Then he was struck by the depression of 1922, which is in the very dim and distant past now but which effectively put a number of people out of work, including myself. The veteran of the first world war went through the long drawn out depression of the thirties, the world wide depression which caused such a great diminution of trade and activity. The result was that the first world war veteran, even if he had recovered some of the ground he had lost during his service from 1914 to

War Veterans Allowance Act 1918, was barely established by 1929 or 1930 when disaster fell upon the country.
Then, following that great depression, of course, there was the second world war. Many of our first world war veterans have therefore had the full course in their lifetime. They went through the first world war, the great depression and many of them had the opportunity and willingly assisted in one way or another during the second world war. Many of them, of course, suffered the grievous losses of their sons in the second world war. Hence for the first world war veteran now getting on in years a grateful country cannot do more than provide assistance. That is precisely what the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act are for, namely to make sure that those who risked their lives in the service of their country should not suffer during their declining years. A very distinguished leader of this country at one time said this:
Our duty to the returned men, their dependents, and the dependents of those who have not come back is clear... It is a demand that we treat their requests with generosity, which is more than mere justice. To the men who sacrificed their all in that fight for freedom we owe all the freedom we have today; though we default the interest on the national debt (which would mean national bankruptcy), we cannot afford to let one of our returned men or their dependents suffer.
That statement was quoted by a distin-gished citizen of Canada and a former member of this House of Commons, namely Mr. L. J. Ladner; and he was quoting from a speech of Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. At that time-and this is in 1930-Mr. Ladner said this:
That statement of the Prime Minister merely reflected the prevailing sentiment and the great impulse of generosity and sense of duty which at that time animated the Canadian people.
I trust that the same spirit animates the Canadian people of the present day. We have passed through a second great world war and there is no one in Canada now who is not familiar with the peril in which this country stood at that time.
We have had the Korean war, in which many of our young men served, and we are fully aware of the services being performed by our men in the navy, army and air force in various dangerous posts abroad. All this service on behalf of Canada has maintained for us the freedom which we enjoy; the freedom to debate here in the House of Commons and on occasion to appear to be fairly annoyed with each other. But it is a bloodless type of fighting; we do it by words. It is only because of the sacrifices of our men in warfare, in the first and second world wars particularly, that we are able to carry on


here in the House of Commons the parliamentary system and maintain the system of democracy which means so much to us.
It is on behalf of the men who served in those wars that I am bringing to the attention of the committee tonight this resolution dealing with the War Veterans Allowance Act, and I hope it will receive the approval of the committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members are very happy to have this legislation introduced at this session. We of the official opposition welcome it very heartily and we hope it will receive a speedy passage through all its stages and be made effective in a very short period of time.
As the minister has pointed out, no matter to which party we belong or on what side of the house we sit, we are all non-partisan when the welfare of our veterans is under consideration. Since we are so completely agreed on this principle there seems to be no need for any extended debate either on the principle of this resolution or even on the principle of the bill at second reading.
The minister has told us-and I welcome this information-that after the bill is introduced to the house it will be sent to the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs. I am sure it will there receive, as always, very sympathetic consideration and many useful suggestions will be made which will improve it and make it more suitable for the conditions it is designed to meet.
As the minister pointed out last evening and again tonight, the original War Veterans Allowance Act dates back to 1930. The objectives of this legislation were very neatly summed up in the original resolution which the minister put on the record tonight. That resolution was introduced in the house by the hon. member for Kootenay, the Hon. J. H. King, minister of pensions and national health in the cabinet of the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King, on March 4, 1930.
The present resolution seeks to bring about the following further changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act. It seeks to increase the rates of war veterans allowance and the permissible income ceilings. It forecasts changes in property and income exemptions, and it will modify certain conditions of eligibility and service.
The minister sounded very magnanimous in his remarks this evening and I hope that when the bill is introduced we will find that its scope has been extended to include the members of the Newfoundland forestry units of world war II, the merchant navy, the rescue tug service, the firefighters and other groups which have not yet been covered by

this legislation. All these bodies have a strong claim to the benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
As hon. members know-it has been pointed out in this house more than once-the Newfoundland foresters of world war II are excluded merely on account of a technicality. Then we have members of the merchant navy who served their country well and are now in need of some sort of assistance which can very well be provided under this act. These people gave valuable service to their country in a time of great need, a service that was duly recognized as essential. As a result of that service they today find themselves incapacitated, unable to support themselves and their families and reduced to dependence upon public relief and charity.
I hope the minister will also see fit to include the British-Canadian veterans who served in India and Afghanistan. The minister mentioned the veterans of the South African War. As recently as this morning, in the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, evidence was given about these British Canadian Veterans who served on the firing line in India. I also hope that the 365-day requirement for veterans of world war I will be abolished.
I think it may be worth while to again repeat the original 1930 resolution which the minister has already put on the record. It reads as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting allowances to war veterans, to provide assistance for certain veterans who are not in receipt of pensions, or who, if in receipt of pensions, are only partially pensionable, or who are unemployable, and to provide for the administration, amounts, terms and conditions of such allowances, and for the payment of such sums as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the proposed legislation.
When we consider the categories I have just mentioned, in the light of that resolution I think it is very clear that it was specially designed to take care of these particular kinds of cases. I say this because the emphasis in the resolution is on veterans and not on any particular grouping, organization or unit in which they may have served.
As far as my own province is concerned, certainly the War Veterans Allowance Act is much more useful and could benefit a great many more people than the Pension Act. There are a number of persons in my province who served their country, as I said, in the forestry unit, the merchant marine and other services who would now find it almost impossible to qualify for a pension under the Pension Act because they do not have the documentation necessary to relate their disability to war service.
I suppose the key word in the original resolution is the word "veteran". I think that 90205-6-311i
War Veterans Allowance Act some of these people have possibly been excluded because we have chosen to place a certain interpretation on that word. I think in the light of the experiences of two wars and particularly of the last war we should be more liberal in our interpretation of what constitutes a veteran and think not so much of the particular unit in which a man served but of the service that he gave to his country and whether his country now has any obligation to him at a time when he is unable to look after himself. It seems to me not only a tragedy but a matter for shame that any person who has served his country and who is disabled should have to resort to public relief. I do not think this was the spirit of the intention of the people who introduced the original resolution.
As I said earlier, I see no reason why there should be any extended debate on this resolution. There is nothing controversial about it. We are all in complete accord with it. We realize that increases in the war veterans allowance rates and income ceilings as well as adjustments to property ceilings are necessary for two reasons, in the first place to bring the veterans allowance payments in line with increases which have taken place in the cost of living and, second, to restore the relationship in the scale of benefits as between war veterans allowances and pensions which existed prior to the recent pension increase. We recognize, as the minister himself has pointed out, that the recent increase in pension rates has made the introduction of this legislation almost imperative in order to restore benefits to those 1,300 pensioners who lost their W.V.A. and other benefits such as hospitalizations when the pension increases came into effect. These adjustments to the War Veterans Allowance Act will put them back on the same footing as they held before the increase was made in the pension rates.
We give this resolution our complete support and hope it will receive swift passage through the house. We shall certainly co-operate to the fullest extent with the government to achieve that result.
