speechtext:
Dr. King was a friend of my father's and of our family and I therefore have a personal knowledge of his interest in this question and of his interest in veterans generally. On that account he was well thought of by the veterans of the Kootenay area and he will be long remembered by those who knew him in pioneer days.
Since that time there has been a steady and somewhat gradual improvement in the legislation, usually as a result of representations from veterans organizations but to some extent because of the experience gained by those responsible for administering the law. The minister invited members to make suggestions with respect to improving this legislation. Mr. Chairman, I accept that invitation with alacrity and I intend to make a few suggestions on that account as well as to make a few general observations upon the legislation.
The minister failed to disclose the prize packet in full. He took the lid off and gave us an indication of the contents, arousing our curiosity without satisfying it by giving us details. I presume we must wait until the bill is introduced before we can satisfy our curiosity. However, I am confident that many veterans and their dependents have looked forward to the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act particularly in recent months in the expectation that they will make their lives a little easier and a little more comfortable. There is no doubt about it that the Legion and other veterans' organizations, with their knowledge of the circumstances of individuals, are concerned about the needs of their members. On that account this is a subject which has been discussed very generally in the last year or two in Legion branches, at provincial conventions and at dominion conventions. As a result, resolutions have been adopted and recommendations made by the representatives of the dominion Canadian Legion and other national officers to the federal government and to the standing committee on veterans affairs. In addition, I am sure, hon. members of this house have received a voluminous correspondence.
I wish to express my agreement, for once, with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo when he said that the general spirit of the veterans' affairs committee is non-partisan. That, I

Since the minister did extend a kind invitation, I am looking forward to the introduction of the bill. I do want to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the Canadian Legion-and other organizations made similar proposals-has been interested in certain particular aspects of this legislation. So far as rates are concerned-and this is a very important thing in the case of the War Veterans Allowance Act; it is the foundation of the act-how much are you going to pay? In its representations to the parliamentary committee last year on the War Veterans Allowance Act the Legion said:
In order to ensure that war veterans allowance recipients do not continue to suffer as living costs advance-the Canadian Legion recommends-
That the rate for married recipients be increased to at least $140 per month and that a comparative adjustment be made in the rate of a single recipient.
When the bill is introduced we hope that it will meet the requests of the Canadian Legion based on the needs of the veterans and their dependents.
Then we come to the question of ceilings which is related to permissive income. In its brief the Legion deals with this question and the necessity for an increase in the ceiling to meet certain particular circumstances. This is the result of experience. You can adopt legislation with the best of intentions. I have been a member of the committee since 1945, and I know of the numerous amendments that were required, and I am sure other hon. members have had the same experience over the years of overlooking something that you did not expect; you did not anticipate a certain situation. I have had that problem particularly brought to my attention with respect to married veterans and common law wives and that sort of thing. Experience has made it necessary to amend legislation that had been considered quite satisfactory years before. Anyway, in connection with the ceilings the Canadian Legion recommends:
That the ceilings on total permissible income under the War Veterans Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year for the single recipient and $2,000 per year for the married recipient.
We hope that when the bill is introduced it will meet the recommendations of the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations.

Then we come to widows' allowance. This has to do with section 30 (11) (b) of the act. The Legion has been very concerned about this and recommends:
That where all other requirements are met, the war veterans allowance board be empowered to declare as eligible widows who would be qualified had the veteran made application during his lifetime.
I have always been interested in widows and their welfare, and I can think of particular instances in my constituency where, because of unforeseen circumstances, the widow of a veteran who served in the same company as I overseas was denied a war veterans allowance because he failed to apply for it during his lifetime. She was not qualified under the present act. I do urge consideration of this matter. I know the cases are few in number. Even though they are few, it is an important matter to the widow concerned.
I come now to the question of the merchant navy personnel. The hon. member preceding me dealt with this question. I can understand his particular interest in the question because he lives in a maritime constituency and would meet more merchant sailors than I would, but I wish to support his representations. I know he supports the representations of the Canadian Legion. In this connection, so far as the merchant navy personnel are concerned, the Canadian Legion recommends:
That the War Veterans Allowance Act be amended to include these veterans of the merchant navy and T.124 service.
There is no necessity to go into details because those who are interested in this legislation know exactly what it means.
I come next to the question of casual earnings. There has been a great improvement in the, shall I say, casual earnings situation over the years. The law, the regulations and the administration in the early days were pretty sticky on this point. It has been improved throughout the years but there is still room for amendment, particularly where you have veterans who have some small fixed income. They cannot earn $50 a month, but they may have $50 a month coming in as interest on a few bonds, and things of that sort. In all fairness I think it is the general opinion of the veterans affairs committee that consideration should be given to situations such as these. Because the Legion has considered this, it submits:
That since it is accepted that recipients are entitled to additional income in excess of the maximum rates and ceilings, the legislation should be amended to provide those recipients, who are unable by reason of ill health to enjoy this advantage, with a single benefit.
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends- that the act be amended to include as exempt income unearned income up to $50 per month for
War Veterans Allowance Act a recipient who is unable because of physical or mental disability to obtain employment.
I think it is a very reasonable recommendation and I trust that the casual earnings regulation will be amended to meet that type of situation.
Then, there is the question of interest on stocks, bonds and so forth. The present act limits to $25 per annum the exemption in respect of interest on bank deposits and bonds and dividends on shares in capital stock. The Legion recommends:
That the act be amended to increase the exemption in respect of interest on bank deposits and bonds and dividends on shares in the capital stock of any company to at least $50.
This is a very modest and responsible recommendation and I do hope the legislation will give it consideration.
There is a section in respect of personal property which is of interest to me, because of the particular circumstances of a number of veterans. The War Veterans Allowance Act from the first has permitted applicants to qualify while in possession of limited personal assets. Since the allowances provide only for minimum living expenditures, it is presumed that the provision in respect of personal property was to cover such eventualities as repairs to a recipient's home, replacement of furniture, medical expenses for dependents, funeral expenses for widows, and so on. This is a rather interesting recommendation:
In 1930 the limits were set at $750 for a single recipient and $1,500 for a married recipient. In 1948 these amounts were increased by $250 to $1,000 for a single recipient and $1,750 for a married recipient. In 1952 there was a further increase of $250 in respect of married recipients bringing the allowance to $2,000.
This shows a gradual improvement in the legislation and the regulations over the years. I continue:
There has been no adjustment whatever during the past eight years and none during the past 12 years in respect of a single recipient.
Therefore the Canadian Legion recommends:
That the personal property exemption be increased to $2,250 for a single recipient and $4,500 for a married recipient.
I hope consideration will be given to this recommendation.
Then we come to world war I Canadians who served in the United Kingdom forces. This has been considered. Representations have been made to the committee on a number of occasions throughout the years. It has been considered by veterans organizations. In this respect the Canadian Legion recommends:
That the act be amended to provide eligibility for those veterans with pre-world war I Canadian

War Veterans Allowance Act domicile who served in the United Kingdom with His Majesty's forces during world war I for at least 365 days prior to the 12th day of November, 1918.
In fact we were discussing this type of situation in the committee today. We hope the question will receive consideration.
Next is the question of world war I service in the United Kingdom. The brief of the Legion contains the following:
The Canadian Legion has in its files the cases of many veterans of world war I who volunteered for service anywhere in the world and who, through no fault of their own, served only in England.
On this account the Legion recommends:
That the act be amended to provide for those veterans who volunteered for active service in any of His Majesty's Canadian forces prior to the coming into force of the Military Service Act in June, 1918, and who served in the United Kingdom during world war I prior to the 12th day of November, 1918.
I think perhaps one of the hon. members from the government benches who will follow me will deal with another aspect of that problem. Then there is the question of eligibility for posthumous pension awards. In that regard the Legion recommends:
That the act be amended to provide that such awards shall be considered to have been in payment prior to the death of the veteran.
Then there is the question of the supplementation of the widows' pension and the Legion recommends as follows:
That the act be amended to provide for supplementation to those widows awarded a widow's pension up to the maximum permissive ceiling under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
That is to allow for a period of adjustment following the death of the husband and for particular circumstances. I trust that recommendation will be given some consideration. Then there is the question of the continuation of married rates which has been discussed on a number of occasions. In that regard the Canadian Legion recommends:
That section 5 (2) be amended to provide for the payment of married rates in such instances if, in fact, he was in receipt of married rates either at the time of the death of the spouse or child, or at any time within the 12 months preceding such death.
That recommendation is based on a few cases that were brought to the attention of the Legion by various branches throughout the country. Then there is the question of dependent's medical expenses which has been a matter that has been advanced by various veterans organizations, has been considered in the committee and has I know, been considered by respective governments. The Canadian Legion recommends as follows:
That the amount of permissible casual earnings be increased by the amount of such medical expenses.

We urge consideration of those representations. Then I want to support the previous speaker who urged consideration of those commonwealth veterans who served in India and on the Afghanistan frontier. That question was brought before the committee this morning by representatives of their organization and we listened to their representations with interest. From what we can gather their number would be very few. It was suggested during the committee hearing that the number possibly would be 50 or something approaching 50. I am not going to deal at length with this matter because I know there is a member on the government side of the house who has previously dealt with this question fully and is well acquainted with it. I happen to have one veteran among my constituents who would be affected if the government saw fit to amend the act to permit those veterans who served in Afghanistan to receive the war veterans allowance.
Finally, I do want to suggest that I believe that veterans or dependents who were in receipt of the war veterans allowance and then went to Great Britain or some other country should receive similar treatment to persons who receive old age security. The veteran or veteran's dependent has to return to Canada and reside for a year in this country and then if they wish they may return to the United Kingdom or some other country after qualifying for the allowance again as a result of 12 months' residence in Canada.
I had a case brought to my attention just before Christmas of the widow of a veteran who served in my company in the first world war who had been in receipt of the war veterans allowance in Canada for a number of years. Prior to the 1960 amendment to the act that made it possible for a recipient to draw the allowance and live outside Canada, this widow had returned to the United Kingdom. When she heard about the amendment she was very anxious to take advantage of it so her brother lent her the money to return to Canada in order that she would be able to spend a year here. She will be here until next January. On arrival in Canada she requalified for the allowance within two weeks but she has to spend a year here before she can return to the United Kingdom.
I suggest that where the record can be easily ascertained and there is no question of qualifying, shall I say, where there has been a clear-cut award of the allowance to a veteran or to a widow, the widow or veteran should not be required to return to Canada and reside here for 12 months. I think such cases could be handled by the administrator of the Department of Veterans Affairs in London. The veteran or widow could go

there and be interviewed by the appropriate official and qualify where it is a straightforward case.
I urge the minister to give consideration to an amendment that would avoid this unnecessary expense on the part of these persons. I think it is an unnecessary expense and in my opinion we should treat veterans and their dependents at least on an equal basis with those who qualify for old age security but who in some cases by no stretch of the imagination have fought in defence of Canada or have made the contribution that the wife of the veteran has made during his service overseas or has made since on account of the veteran's disabilities. In cases like that of the member for Kootenay West with his advancing years, his fidgetiness and crankiness and so on, I think the woman is entitled to some consideration and should be given consideration in these situations. I urge the minister to give consideration to that aspect of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I have reviewed the major recommendations of the Canadian Legion. I have little more to say at this time except that I must say that although the work on the veterans affairs committee sometimes does not appeal to some members, the intellectuals, shall I say, I think that those members who have served on the committee throughout the years have got a great deal of pleasure out of it because it does provide an opportunity to keep in close touch with the question of the needs and welfare of veterans and their dependents. That close contact and the time spent studying these matters at least gives a feeling of satisfaction that he has tried to do a little something for his comrades and their dependents.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this measure which is so important to veterans, a measure which I am sure is of interest not only to the veterans of this house but to all other members as well. There is an inscription on a soldier's grave in southern England in these words:
God and the soldier
Men alike adore
When at the brink of danger,
Not before.
The danger o'er-both are alike requited,
God is forgot
And the brave soldier slighted.
The brave soldier slighted. I am sure the majority of Canadians feel that the veterans legislation of this country brought into effect over the last 40 or 50 years is certainly second to none in the whole world. That of course is as it should be because
War Veterans Allowance Act Canadians' record of service and sacrifice in the wars of freedom has been second to none as well.
I should like to compliment the Minister of Veterans Affairs on the energy and the understanding that he has brought to this department. He follows in the wake of many able ministers who have rendered distinguished service in this most important portfolio. Since we are dealing with war veterans allowances, I should like to compliment the minister also on the appointment recently of the new chairman to that board. In bringing Colonel W. T. Cromb to this board from western Canada, he brought a man who has distinguished himself in war and in peace, in the service of his country. Over the last few months, I have found he has given every sympathy and every consideration to the cases I have brought to him and his board, and, I am sure, to the cases of others.
Like most other members in this house, I suppose there is hardly a day goes by that each of us does not have a case of a veteran or a veteran's dependent come across our desks. Perhaps those of us who come from the maritimes-I say this in complete humility-have a few more cases than do members from other parts of Canada. For whatever reason, we seem to have had more men and women serving in the Canadian forces proportionately than any other part of Canada. I think the record will bear me out. Perhaps we could get into an argument about that. Our war casualties were heavy and, therefore, we seem to be getting more and more cases as the years go by. I know of families in which every man enlisted. I know of one case which six sons went to the war and five were killed. I know of one family in which eight sons went overseas and some never came home. I knew one community particularly well, because I was teaching there at the time, in which every able-bodied man enlisted. Only the youngsters and the old people were left at home. These men served in Hong Kong, France, Italy, at sea and in the air. Many of them were killed and wounded.
This is a most welcome measure, not only to those who are receiving war veterans allowance but to all Canadians. The present scale is $120 for a married recipient. They may then receive, under most necessitous circumstances, an additional $25 from the assistance fund. We know, of course, that this amount does not provide for the necessities of life, let alone the luxuries. In order to be fair, we must admit that the sum does provide a few of the necessities but it does not go far enough.

War Veterans Allowance Act
When the Pension Act was amended recently many letters were written to us from pensioners who were receiving small pensions. I am sure all hon. members received such letters. Of course, the pensions were increased but because of the ceiling on war veterans allowances the income of these veterans did not increase at all. Some of the letters were worded rather strongly. Although there were no aspersions cast upon my ancestry, some of these letters cast some aspersions upon our ability to benefit the veterans of this country. Most of these veterans will be taken care of by this amendment.
We are all familiar, of course, with the conditions of service required to qualify under the War Veterans Allowance Act. A veteran must have served in a theatre of war or, if not in a theatre of war, he must have enlisted in both wars or be in receipt of a small pension. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West, referred to the 365 days of service in England which are necessary in order to qualify for an allowance. This provision has been given considerable attention in past years. England was not considered a theatre of war for those who went overseas in the 1914-1918 war, but it was in the second world war. I had referred to me a while ago the case of an old man who had served for 11J months in England. He was, therefore, unable to qualify and did not receive the allowance which he badly needed. He was furious and his people were furious, but there was nothing we could do.
I suppose hon. members will ask whether or not that provision is going to be changed. I think the time is rapidly approaching when it should be changed. As has been pointed out, the average age of the men who served in the first war is now about 70. There may be a few who are 60, but they would have been in their early teens when they enlisted. Old soldiers never die, they just fade away. It is regrettable, but they are rapidly fading away now. If we are going to do anything for these men who, through no fault of their own, just got as far as England in world war I, it should be done now.
We can go too far with this idea of the welfare state, and we most likely will. However, we are dealing here with a very special group of Canadians. I would, therefore, urge the minister to be as generous as possible.
The minister put on the record some statistics from the annual report of the department. I should like to put a few more statistics on the record, that are of interest.
Before going further, I should like to compliment the minister upon the annual report turned out by his department. The


content is good; it is factual and I like the way the report is bound, with the name on the cover. I think this is the way the annual reports of all government departments should be bound at the end of each year.
The number of cases that have been approved over the years is rather interesting. In 1930 the act was brought into force, as the minister pointed out, and in that year there were approximately 2,000 cases approved. This figure remained steady until 1939 when there were 4,336 cases approved. It is interesting to note that the number of cases approved in the years 1939 to 1945 dropped off. In some years there were only about 1,000 eases approved. What was happening there? It is very plain to see that these men who had fought in world war I and who had been badly used up, rallied to the service of their country in 1939. We all know of cases of men who were badly wounded in world war I who were drawing pensions but who re-enlisted to serve their country. We find, therefore, that up until 1945 the number of cases approved was very small. In 1945 and 1946 the number of cases approved for war veterans allowances began to increase very rapidly. From 1950 to 1960 the number of cases has maintained a constant level at about 12,000 per year.
There is an interesting fact that came to my attention when I did my research on this subject. The number of first world war veterans is slowly declining. This means, of course, as I said earlier, that first world war veterans are regrettably leaving the scene, the numbers of widows and orphans on strength is still holding up. In 1960, as of March 31, the number of oases, that is for veterans and widows, stood at 67,683. While the minister did not give the figures, I think the records will show that the steady growth of cases will increase about 3,000 more this year. Now, if the veterans of the first war are declining in numbers, then evidently the increase must be coming from those who served in world war II. I have endeavoured without much success in the last year or two to ascertain from an actuarial point of view just when the peak would be reached in connection with war veterans allowance. No one has been able to tell me. I suppose it is because there are so many unknown factors, so many imponderables. However, it would appear that about 1980 we will reach the peak of pension cases and veterans allowance cases.
There are a number of other interesting factors concerning approvals in the last year that I should like to put on the record. The veterans of world war I, South Africa and the Northwest field force numbered 3,068 and reinstatements numbered 2,749. The number of approvals for veterans of world war II

and Korea amounted to 1,668, and reinstatements, 971. The dual service allowances, that is for men who served in both world wars but who did not serve in a theatre of war, numbered 103 and reinstatements, 42. The number of approvals for commonwealth and allied forces amounted to 932, with 449 reinstatements.
I should like to query the minister on one point. I do not expect an immediate answer on this. As the hon. member who has just spoken mentioned in his concluding remarks, I too wish to compliment the minister on bringing in this legislation at this time. I wish to point out that when the legislation was initially brought in in 1930, it was brought in in order to deal with a specific situation with regard to the veterans of that day who found themselves in increasing need and who were not eligible under the terms of the Pension Act as administered by the pension commission. I would venture to say that a sentence in the brief presented by the Canadian Legion to the Prime Minister and the cabinet applies then as it does now, namely that the war veterans were compelled to pay the same prices-and probably high prices-for goods and services as were all other people and consequently the government of the day saw fit to support this group of veterans in that way.
We all have agreed that legislation of this particular type is not contentious and the request has been made by a number of veterans that it be expeditiously dealt with. I feel that the veterans of the country deserve a voice here in the House of Commons probably more than we at times are prepared to give them and do in fact give them. Consequently I am going to make some reference to some of the remarks that have been made previously in the house. I hope that no pressure will be brought to bear on any member of the House of Commons to terminate the discussion at this resolution stage.
This may be in some respects somewhat irrelevant, Mr. Chairman, on the other hand it has a very direct bearing on the discussion as we proceed in my opinion. On a previous occasion when another piece of pension legislation was being amended, I made some remarks in this house. I do not say this in

War Veterans Allowance Act order to take advantage of the situation this evening nor do I speak with any political implication because, as a veteran myself I certainly feel that such legislation and discussion should not be contentious. In my brief years here as a representative of the people and of veterans, I have found that lip service is sometimes paid to this particular part of the question, but is not so much in evidence in other quarters in our operations here in the House of Commons. In speaking in the house on February 5, 1961- and I quote from page 1861 of Hansard- I said this to the minister at that time:
-and I am sure he will in the not too distant future-introduce similar amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I made that statement without the knowledge that this resolution to amend the act would be forthcoming at this time and with the sincere hope and desire that the purpose for which the resolution has been introduced will be served. I feel in this way about it. Many veterans who are in receipt of war veterans allowance today, in my view, should be recipients under the Pension Act as administered by the pension commission. I say that for this reason. In 1939-40, when as very young men many students were accepted by the authorities of that day, they were not asked what their disability was. As a matter of fact they were not examined too closely. They were not made any promises either. They were taken for the service they could render. The men with whom I served performed this service with the full knowledge of what the price might be, without asking what the return would be or what awards might be made.
Therefore I feel that when a decision is rendered adversely against a veteran, where he has indicated that the problem with which he is confronted is attributable to a condition which existed prior to enlistment, my sympathies always lean on the side of the veteran.
Where a situation exists when a veteran becomes incapable of earning his own livelihood following his service due to a condition which is not attributable to service, I am always inclined to examine that veteran's background and experience and try to determine in my own mind what would happen to any of us under those circumstances. I can assure this committee that in many cases these people are possibly not being dealt with as fairly as I personally feel they should be. These are very serious matters to my mind and hon. members would be surprised at the number of such cases with which we have to deal.
It certainly is not a very enviable thing to examine these situations and review them.

Nevertheless I can assure the committee that I and these veterans who are now and will be recipients of war veterans allowance are extremely grateful for the measure that is being presented.
If I may, I should like to refer to another matter. This is a situation that was created on another occasion in connection with a statement made in the house in reply to a question put to the Minister of Veterans Affairs by the hon. member for Trinity. The hon. member observed:
I wish to draw to the attention of the committee the necessity, in considering this item, to consider the revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act. The changes which were recently made in the Pension Act have resulted in pensioners being cut off from the supplements provided by the war veterans allowance and, worse than that, these pensioners no longer receive certain medical benefits which were previously available to them.
I should like to suggest that the committee urge upon the government an early reconsideration of the War Veterans Allowance Act so that these people, who in many cases are very much in need, will receive proper consideration.
To the best of my knowledge this hon. member is not a member of the veterans affairs committee. This certainly does not exclude him from the privilege of asking this question of the minister. Immediately following that statement I said to the committee:
I should like to say to the committee that this suggestion was made on numerous occasions during the consideration of the amendments to the Pension Act. If one refers to Hansard, one will find that this request was made by most hon. members who spoke.
Here is the way in which political advantage is taken by some hon. members. I do not say this because the hon. member to whom I am referring is not in the committee, nor do I make the next statement with any motive, but this may be the only opportunity I have of speaking in this regard.
I should like to refer for a moment or two to the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on veterans affairs. I refer to the evidence contained in the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 6 dated February 23, 1961. This recommendation was moved by the hon. member for Renfrew North and was seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West:
This committee recommends that the government give consideration to the advisability of amending clause 13 by deleting the words "in respect of any period before the first day of the month next following the day on which this act is assented to" and substituting therefor the words "in respect of any period before the first day of January, 1961".

speechtext:
Before I begin my brief remarks, may I say how delighted I am that you should be occupying the chair. Knowing that modesty is one of your many qualities, I wish to take this opportunity to place on record for the benefit of your constituents in Winnipeg South that you have on other occasions taken over the duties of chairman of the committee and discharged in a most exemplary manner the heavy responsiblities of that office. Lest hon. members think I may be prejudiced in your favour, let me say at once that the fact you are my colleague, my neighbour and the godfather of my twins has nothing whatsoever to do with it.


Earlier this year the Minister of Veterans Affairs addressed a public meeting in Vancouver and in answer to a question from someone in his audience replied that the government was deeply aware of the hardships facing those in receipt of war veterans allowances even though the War Veterans Allowance Act had been amended as recently as 1957. Subsequently some misgivings were expressed in certain quarters that notwithstanding the sympathetic interest shown by the minister the government had no intention of doing anything to alleviate the situation. I am therefore very happy that the minister has introduced this resolution, because it is an indication that the representations made by the private members of this party have borne fruit and that this government has indeed kept faith with the veterans of Canada.
As one who has served on the standing committee on veterans affairs since my election to this house in 1957 I take great satisfaction with regard to what we have done for the veterans. I know that many veterans in my riding will welcome this resolution. I have at least three branches of the Canadian Legion in my riding and there is another organization of which I am particularly proud because it is unique in Canada. I refer to the organization known as the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada, Pacific group No. 280, Chinese Canadians. This organization has as its life president Her Majesty the Queen, and to my knowledge this group, composed of over 200 Chinese Canadian veterans many of whom served with me and are my friends from boyhood, is the only unit of its kind in Canada and is another indication that Chinese Canadians have served their country in war as well as their fellow Canadians.
This unit will be holding its fourteenth annual meeting in Vancouver on Sunday, May 28, and I am sure that all hon. members will want to join with me in extending congratulations to this unit and in expressing the hope that their contribution, which was so worth while in time of war, will continue to an even greater degree in time of peace.
In the brief presented to the Prime Minister and the cabinet by the Canadian Legion on December 12, 1960, some seven pages out of 40 were devoted to proposed amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. In dealing with the War Veterans Allowance Act the Canadian Legion discussed increases in rates and ceilings; allowances for widows and orphans outside of Canada; widow's allowance payable under section 30(11) (b); merchant navy personnel; casual earnings; interest on stocks and bonds; personal property; eligibility for posthumous awards and supplementation of widows' pension.

In his remarks tonight the minister covered three of these subjects, namely increases in the monthly rates of allowance and income ceiling, further exemptions in property and income and modification of certain conditions of service eligibility. I am sure the increase in rates and ceilings will be welcomed by all but for some time, Mr. Chairman, I have been particularly troubled by the plight of the wife of a veteran who is receiving war veterans allowance because in one particular field, namely that of medical treatment, the wife is not covered. In theory the veteran receiving the allowance could quite easily and conceivably spend all of his pension in paying for the medical treatment of his wife who might have spent 10, 20, 30 or more years in looking after him and who by reason of advanced age is no longer in a position to work. This situation distresses me because without the assistance of his wife the veteran might have been in a very bad predicament. I would therefore suggest that some consideration be given to the advisability of extending medical treatment to the wives of those veterans who are drawing war veterans allowance so that this very heavy financial burden may be taken from the shoulders of those who can ill afford to carry it.
I want to emphasize that I understand the principle that medical coverage and treatment facilities under the act are designed only for veterans and therefore civilians do not qualify. None the less I think a very good case can be made out for the wives and widows of pensioners and other qualified persons. I also realize that practically every province in Canada has its own hospital insurance plan under which many people are covered. However, I still feel there are gaps which must be filled from the resources of the federal government. I am hopeful that a national health plan will be implemented by this government. If this is done the problem with which I am concerned will disappear. However, until such time as a national health plan is established I feel there is some urgency in providing medical treatment for wives and widows who have been of so much help to their husbands.
I wish to conclude by saying that much as I appreciate the proposed increase in the rates and ceilings now payable, I know that within a short time representations will again be made for a further increase. The complaint will be advanced that the level of payment is not keeping up with the rise in the cost of living. I would therefore make a suggestion not only to the Minister of Veterans Affairs but also to all members of the government that henceforth when consideration has to be given to an increase in pensions of this kind, rather than grant the increase in one
War Veterans Allowance Act lump sum we settle on an amount which will be adequate by present-day standards and also make the provision that any increases henceforth will be based on the cost of living index.
It may well be that this index will fluctuate from province to province, but I think that if we can supplement the basic rate, which is a reasonable and decent one, with a payment to cover the increased cost of living we will remove any need to have continual representations made because provision could be made for a periodic review by the war veterans allowance board. I think this proposal is sound. It would remove any possibility of increases of this kind in pensions being used as a political football.
To me, Mr. Chairman, there is something rather pathetic and repugnant about veterans delegations coming to Ottawa year after year pleading for an increase. By granting an increase we recognize the validity of their claim. If we could attach a provision for the payment of a sum to keep pace with the cost of living index we would all be spared the criticism that pensions are inadequate. Parliament would still have control over those funds because parliament would have to vote the necessary sum to cover those ancillary payments. Therefore there would be an opportunity for full discussion. Even with such a provision the payment would still lag behind the cost of living, but if there was a yearly review the gap would not be so disproportionate.
I have other remarks to make but I shall defer them until a more suitable stage of the proceedings. In the meantime I wish once again to congratulate the minister and this government for again keeping their promises.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, usually I do not take up much time in speaking and seldom do I speak on a resolution preceding a bill. This may be owing to the fact that I would rather sit back and listen to others express their ideas from which I may learn. But I do feel I should say a few words on this resolution. One reason is that at the time the amendments to the Pension Act were before the house several members-I do not refer to opposition members in particular- rather implied afterwards that I was not in favour of granting increases to those recipients of war veterans allowance. This is quite wrong and is one reason why I felt I should say something on the resolution stage.
I suppose my trouble at the time, and it always has been, and I hear a great deal about it, is that these are two distinct acts. The people who are in receipt of a disability pension have always claimed to me that they felt they earned it. Those members who are
4934	HOUSE OF
War Veterans Allowance Act on the veterans affairs committee and were fortunate enough to be at the committee hearing the other day know that we had a delegation before us. The spokesman for that delegation made it very clear to us that those veterans who were in receipt of disability pensions really felt that they earned those pensions a little bit more than other veterans have earned theirs.
There may be an element of boastfulness in that feeling and I suppose that is the way I felt in expressing myself at the time we were dealing with that legislation. Now we are dealing with an act which provides assistance for a group of veterans who, regardless of their service, deserve assistance. The group to which this legislation applies is that group of men who at one time in their lives were willing to take the chances of any other soldier. Many of them were fortunate enough to go through the first world war and the second world war without catching a "blighty" as we used to say in the first world war or without incurring any disability that was disclosed by an examination, and these men did not receive a pension. While they were fortunate, there is no doubt that if men spend two or three years in the service, especially in strenuous positions in the front lines, there is a deterioration and disability does exist to some extent.
In any case, the veterans allowance legislation was brought into being to help those veterans who, probably through no fault of their own, found it difficult to re-establish themselves or who encountered sickness or trouble. In many cases they lacked education and some of them suffered from unfortunate circumstances such as may happen to all of us. These people arrive at a time in life when they cannot fit into a position where they can make a living. This legislation is for that group of people. I should like to say, and I mean it, that my heart goes out to all people, whether or not they are veterans, who find themselves in such a condition in the later years of their lives. These people have got to receive assistance from the rest of us who are fortunate enough to be able to maintain ourselves, pay our taxes and possibly lay a little bit aside.
As far as the veterans are concerned, as other members have said this evening I think they deserve special attention. I remember that in 1955, I believe, the then minister of veterans affairs initiated a thorough review of this act. The principle was established that a man who had seen service was aged ten years and provision was made to pay him the old age pension ten years earlier. As time has gone by and more consideration has been given to these veterans, benefits have been added until we have reached the point where
[Mr. Montgomery.!

an unmarried man or woman is allowed to have an income up to $1,000 including the war veterans allowance.
It was brought very forcibly to the attention of members of the committee and to all members of the house no doubt for the first time that in the vicinity of 13,000 veterans who had been receiving both a disability pension and the veterans allowance would get no benefit if the two acts were not amended in the same year. I know that all members of the committee felt the same way regardless of the party to which they belonged. They felt that we must endeavour to have the War Veterans Allowance Act amended this year so that those who had been in receipt of benefits under both acts would still be able to receive these benefits.
As others have done, I should like to pay my compliments to the minister because I know he has worked hard to get these amendments before the house. I am very glad they have been brought forward. I do not really think it is necessary for me to correct any impression that people may have got from the attitude they thought I had, but I really believe that war veterans allowance recipients deserve benefits far more than some disability pensioners because the disability pensioners do have a preference so far as many things are concerned. This group of veterans does not get a preference.
I suppose this is not the right place to mention it but 1 hope I am here when the amendments to the Civil Service Act are brought forward. A case involving a veteran brought this situation very forcibly to my attention. A man with some four years service in the second world war returned from service and he was fortunate in that he was not wounded. He was not disabled in any way and therefore he received no benefits. He came back, married and started a family and had a nice home. Through an unfortunate accident involving a tractor he was killed. The widow was left with three small children, the oldest being about 12 years of age now. She has to go out and work. She is a secretary and, all other things being equal, I think that as the widow of a veteran she should have some preference in civil service examinations.
This is the first time this matter has come to our attention. I can see no reason why a widow of a veteran who is responsible for educating three children and has no other income than that which she can earn should not be given every chance when she wants to go out and work. When she takes a civil service examination she has no preference. She has to take her chance with all the other

secretaries. I just mention that at this time because it does have something to do with veterans.
I should also like to join other members in paying my compliments to the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs with whom I have come in contact. I really think that some of the speeches that were made on the amendments to the other act, to which I know I probably should not refer, did have some effect. I know of some pensions that have been granted in various parts of the country under section 70 where there had been difficulty in securing a pension before, and that is all to the good. As one member has said, there are many veterans in receipt of the veterans allowance who should be drawing nearly a full pension under the Pension Act but their cases could never be thoroughly established.
There is one other point I wish to mention. I have not made any particular study of the problem but I am inclined to think that the time is coming when those men who volunteered to serve in world war I should be permitted to draw war veterans allowance even though they did not get overseas. Actually, I think I could make a list of about 30 cases myself of men who would have given their right arm to get overseas in the second world war. They were kept in camps in Canada because they were good staff men. I do not believe these men should be penalized. I am not making this plea on behalf of the second world war men because a good many of them made good and they are not interested in this measure. However, I do believe that the men who volunteered to serve in world war I and who never got out of Canada should be brought under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I do not believe there are any other points I wish to mention at this time. However, there may be some points I want to mention when I see the bill. Nearly every member has mentioned gaps in the legislation which he hopes will be covered. I do not look for too much. This act and the Pension Act have to be reviewed and brought up to date every few years. I do not know to what extent these amendments will satisfy hon. members. No doubt they will not satisfy me any more than they will satisfy anyone else. We are always going to want something more in the act.
It seems to me there will be something for the veterans affairs committee to study every year. A delegation appeared before our committee this morning to present several resolutions. Just as we started the representative said that he was going to remove some of the resolutions because he understood that legislation which had been passed or was
War Veterans Allowance Act before the house met some of the points referred to in their representations. I feel this is a rather encouraging sign to find that resolutions which were drawn by organizations four or five months ago have already been covered by legislation. I believe the disability pensioners in my area are fairly happy. I think the war veterans allowance group will be happy too. There will be some veterans who will not be covered by this measure unless there is some change in the period necessary for qualification. Those veterans who did not get in enough time overseas are going to be disappointed. The department, the minister and the government, in their wisdom will have to decide just what extension can be given. I think we must be thankful for what we do get for the veterans. I am sure the veterans who will be in receipt of these increases will be thankful. However, we will go on fighting for more if we do not get enough.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, near the conclusion of what the hon. member who just sat down said, he made a reference to certain observations he might wish to make when he had seen the bill. I know how keen the Minister of Veterans Affairs is in his other capacity as leader of the house to get on with the business of the house, particularly these non-contentious measures, as quickly as possible without abridging anyone's right to make any suggestions, particularly on this kind of legislation. It does occur to me, sir, that it might facilitate the work, not just of the committee but of the house, if I said publicly what I have indicated privately to the minister, that is that I think I can speak for my friends on this side of the house when I say that if the minister would like, before the conclusion of this evening's sitting, to bring this stage to an end and ask for unanimous consent to go on with second reading of the bill, we would be willing to do so. I am not saying that there would not still be a debate on second reading, but we could get started on that debate by the end of this evening and perhaps get closer to the stage when this legislation would come into operation. I think I can speak for my friends on this side of the house when I say that we are ready to co-operate in that respect.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF ALLOWANCES AND INCOME CEILINGS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like at once to join with those who have congratulated the minister on assuming his new post. I do so as a former fellow officer of the Canadian armoured corps. I can assure the minister that the members of his old corps throughout Canada are proud to find one from our branch of the service in the role of Minister of Veterans

War Veterans Allowance Act Affairs. They feel, as I do, that the resolution the minister has brought forward tonight is of vital importance.
At the outset, I should like to draw attention to a few of the statistics which the minister mentioned in his opening remarks. It is a fact that over 12,000 war veteran allowance recipients reside in the province of British Columbia. This is somewhat over one fifth of the total in Canada, and if we calculated population on the basis of this distribution, the population of our province should be close to 3,700,000. This is far from the case. I mention this fact just to try to emphasize how vitally important this war veterans allowance legislation is to the people of British Columbia, far more so than to any other province in this dominion.
It has not been the privilege of all members during the past three years to serve on the veterans affairs committee. I happen to be one of those members who have not been so privileged.
The cost of living in urban areas has had an influence on the distribution of this heavy population of war veterans allowance pensioners in British Columbia. As a result of a desire on the part of many veterans in the prairies to move to a milder climate, many of them have come to the greater Vancouver area. Shortly thereafter, they find living costs are prohibitive. These pensioners have, therefore, moved up the coast. Those of us who are in the coastal regions up the coast from Vancouver therefore find in our area an inordinately high percentage of the 12,000 war veterans allowance recipients residing in British Columbia.
As I said earlier I have not been privileged to serve as a member of the war veterans committee so, as a member who represents literally thousands of war veterans allowance recipients, I should like to call attention to a few major points. I can assure the minister and you, Mr. Chairman, that those who are in receipt of war veterans allowances are grateful for this worth while and logically administered program. However, because of the cost of living, their interest has been great in seeing an increase in the amount of the pension.
I can assure you that the many hundreds and even into the thousands whom I represent will wish me to convey to the minister their gratefulness on seeing this change come into being. I think it is perhaps safe to say that nowhere else in Canada are these pensioners faced with living costs which make this change so urgent and so necessary. Many of those throughout my riding have discussed at some length the ceilings on their earnings. It is with great pleasure again tonight that we

learned the minister has indicated that adjustment upwards in the ceiling will be established by the new legislation.
There is, however, one point which I should most meticulously like to draw to the attention of this committee at this time. I refer to the W.V.A. recipient over the age of 70 and his position with relation to the old age security pension. If it can be done, and if it is financially feasible, it would certainly be appreciated if the war veterans allowance recipients after the age of 70 were able to receive old age security benefits, as are pensioners from industry and other walks of life who have reached that retiring age, without in any way reducing their basic war veterans allowance.
I should like to join with my colleague from Vancouver Centre who discussed the situation of medical treatment and hospital care for the wives and the widows of war veterans allowance pensioners. I do this without criticism of this government. I feel it is well to point the finger where the finger should be pointed. In this case I refer to the regulations under the public health and welfare branch of the province of British Columbia. I would urge the minister and his department to make contact with them in a spirit of cooperation and good will in order to ascertain whether the province of British Columbia cannot do something in a fair and equitable way to see that these wives and widows are treated as are the wives and widows of all other nonwar veterans allowance pensioners. I think this is a charge against the provincial government which they would be prepared to adjust in order to treat W.V.A. pensioners' wives and widows on an equitable basis provided the facts were strongly brought out and the situations were made known.
There is one other phase of this matter which has 'been discussed I believe by two hon. members who have spoken previously. It has to do with merchant seamen. I think very frequently the situation of merchant seamen is little appreciated or understood by many of those who are resident in areas which are not tidal. During the war many of these chaps were frozen in their positions. Many of them served at sea in Canada's merchant services and had no option, despite their wish to serve in Canada's armed services.
Another common misconception is, of course, that these Canadian merchant seamen benefited with rates of pay and other considerations comparable with those of merchant seamen from the United States. This unfortunately is not the case. Their rates of pay remained in a frozen state based upon the date that their retention was insisted on by arrangements Canada made in many cases with the British admiralty. In the course of

service Canada's merchant seamen visited ports in theatres of active operations. I can take you, I would say quite modestly, to 38 merchant seamen who received severe injuries and wounds who are today incapacitated to a very large degree and are suffering from the services they provided to this nation at a time of dire need. I would urge upon the minister and the members of this committee that fresh thought be given to and a fresh look be taken at our responsibilities to Canada's merchant seamen who saw service, have suffered injury and are incapacitated through serving in active theatres of war.

speechtext:
It is quite true that the hon. gentlemen referred to do on occasion generate a certain amount of heat, but if they accomplish that purpose it will be the only useful purpose they have achieved.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs on this measure and on the other legislation introduced this session.
We had, first, the increase in disability pensions, then the reduction in the amount of land required for small holdings, and this measure completes the triad. When the disability pensions were increased there seemed to be considerable confusion concerning the future of the war veterans allowance. Like many other hon. members, I am sure, I have received representations concerning war veterans allowance. A branch of the Canadian Legion in my riding forwarded me a resolution urging an early revision of this act.
In a constituency such as mine the war veterans allowance is more important than it is in an urban riding. In an urban riding we find people retiring on pensions from the civil service and various employer-employee pension schemes. In a rural area the farmers and fishermen do not have this opportunity to retire on pension and therefore much greater emphasis is placed on war veterans allowance.
I also find that the general public express a great deal of interest in veterans legislation. I find that when people are speaking to me on behalf of veterans or veterans' widows

War Veterans Allowance Act they are most emphatic that these people should receive special treatment because of their contribution to the nation.
In making his remarks the minister requested hon. members to make suggestions concerning improvements in the legislation. One complaint I have received on a number of occasions concerns the 12 month service provision prior to the armistice. I realize there is a great deal of controversy among world war I veterans concerning this qualification, but I believe world war II veterans would appreciate seeing this qualification eliminated or reduced. The number of veterans affected is very small; I understand it is in the vicinity of approximately 5,000. Perhaps the minister could give consideration to either eliminating this qualification or reducing it.
The saddest war veterans allowance cases that I have had drawn to my attention are those of widows of recipients of war veterans allowance. These widows receive the war veterans allowance for a year and then it is discontinued.
It is said that the widow is under 55 years of age and is able to work. However, in a small town, with children, it is difficult to obtain either full or part-time employment. I should like to see consideration given to the allowance being continued to widows, especially in cases where there are small children.
One other complaint I have received concerns the amount of permissible income. The complaints have been that it was not high enough, and formerly there was a monthly limit on the income that could be earned. This situation has been improved and clarified. This has enabled a great many people to earn extra income. It has also allowed a great many qualified people, such as nurses, to return to their professions. Formerly, if a nurse took a case she would be more or less limited to four or five days' nursing; then she would have earned her permissible income for that month and would either have to discontinue attending the patient or have her income deducted from her husband's war veterans allowance.
There are two further points I should like to draw to the minister's attention. The first is that I feel there is too much emphasis placed upon the aspect of permanent disability. A war veteran may develop a severe case of ulcers and be unable to work for a period of, say, a year. But as long as there is hope of him receiving medical treatment and achieving recovery he is not eligible for war veterans allowance. When the veteran is unable to work and has no income, this further aggravates his condition. I think this

applies particularly to ulcer cases. I would appreciate consideration being given to this question.
The other complaint I have received in regard to war veterans allowance and the qualification for permanent disability allowance concerns the type of work available and the skill of the individual. A veteran who is qualified only as a labourer would have a difficult time carrying on with a partial disability. It is true that he could be referred to light work such as operating an elevator, or something of that nature, but in many areas this type of work is not available.
I hope the minister and the war veterans allowance board will pay more attention to this aspect of the legislation in the future. It is fine to say that a veteran can carry on light work, but if he is a labourer, farmer or fisherman it is very difficult for him to obtain light work. I think there could probably be more consideration given to this matter when these cases are being considered.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks at this time will have to be brief. I should like to confine them particularly to a problem concerning a small group of imperial veterans.
However, before I proceed along those lines I should like to congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs for initiating and bringing forward such a full program of benefits and assistance to our war veterans during this session of parliament.
First we had the 20 per cent increase in disability pensions. This was well deserved and well received. We now have this resolution to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act and to grant increases and other benefits which I am sure will be equally well appreciated.
When we look back to the days of the first world war it is interesting to note that the proposed increases to veterans allowance come at a time when the very youngest veterans who saw service at that time will now be 60 years of age, which is the age limit for veterans allowance. It will also provide much needed extra assistance to the elderly veterans and sweeten the declining years of their lives.
This problem I intend to bring up concerns imperial veterans. I brought it up last year and went into it at considerable length. However, I am not going to confuse the issue by reading over a lot of correspondence and different documents I have here on file. I would just like to state briefly that this problem concerns a group of imperial veterans who served on the Afghanistan frontier between 1914 and 1919. The records show there were about 5,000 of them altogether and it is possible there may have been Canadians among

them, at least people who had lived in Canada prior to the war. It will be recalled that a great many Britishers who were here when the war started returned to their native land and joined the regiments with which they had been associated before they came to Canada. This group served on the Afghanistan frontier. There were about 5,000 of them. But there were many thousands of other British or commonwealth troops who served in different parts of India and on the frontier. But this small group of 5,000 did not get the British victory medal and for that reason they were not entitled to war veterans allowance. They received other medals. They received the Afghanistan medal. They received the Indian frontier medal and they also received the general service medal.
I should like to put on record a case with which I am familiar. It is the case of the widow of one of these veterans. Her husband served some 12 years in the imperial forces and, not through his choice, when the war began in 1914 he was sent to the East and he spent his time in India. He was one of this force which was on the Afghanistan frontier. He has passed on now, but his widow is in dire need of assistance and I should like to deal with this particular veteran's widow. Her husband, as I say, had about 12 years' service in the army. He served during the war from 1914 to 1919. He had three medals given to him for active service. He had the red chevron for 1914 and he had the blue ones for 1915, 1916, 1917, 1918, and 1919. Unfortunately he had not been granted the victory medal and for that reason his widow is today not entitled to war veterans allowance.
This lady, who had such an outstanding husband who did not enjoy particularly good health while he was in Canada due to a tropical disease he had contracted while serving in India-malaria and other troubles -is today required to go to the welfare office every two weeks and pick up her welfare cheque. I know there are hundreds if not thousands of women who have to do that. Nevertheless, this is the widow of a veteran who had a very good record of service but due to some misunderstanding this small, group of British veterans he served with did not receive the victory medal and are not entitled to veterans allowances. This lady happens to be one who has to suffer because
Business of the House
of it. As I say, some 5,000 troops were involved in this campaign. I have all the records here but, as I mentioned, I do not want to delay the committee by dealing with them now. My time is about up. Nevertheless this is in my opinion a very worthy case.
According to some estimates there are perhaps 50 of these veterans in Canada today. I do not, myself, think there are as many. I know of three men in southern Ontario. The hon. member for Kootenay West says he knows of one. I know it would be impossible to get the British government today to act and award victory medals to these men now but my suggestion is-and I made it last year and I notice that the British imperial veterans are asking for the same thing-is simply this: I strongly recommend to the minister that the 1914-1919 award of the Indian general service medal be accepted as entitlement to the war veterans allowance as well as the victory medal.
As I say, there is a very small group which would be affected. In dollars it would not amount to very much. Nevertheless it would be of great assistance to those who are suffering simply because there was a mistake made some 40 years ago.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Has a resolution, approved by the director of the trans-Canada alliance of German-Canadians on February 19, 1961, concerning the loss of German and Austrian old age annuities and pensions to German immigrants on becoming Canadian citizens, been received?
2.	If so: (a) what action is requested of the
federal government:	(b) what reply has been
made?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	Yes. Mimeographed copies of a resolution were sent to the Prime Minister and to the ministers of external affairs and National Health and Welfare. The Minister of National Health and Welfare replied on behalf of himself and his colleagues.
2.	(a) The resolution urged the government "to enter into a reciprocal treaty with the government of West Germany and the government of Austria with the intent that no individual's rightful claim to social security from these countries shall be lost by becoming a Canadian citizen."
(b)	The organization was assured that their representations had been carefully noted and would receive most sympathetic consideration in future social security planning.
